events.text: The broad road runs north to the palace gate: three arches of dressed stone, a tower of red pillars, guards in blue. In front of it, where the road widens, there is a stone platform with nobody on it. You climb up and lie down, and the city lies down in front of you: tiled roofs, the bell pavilion, the smoke of ten thousand kitchens, the river, and across the river a mountain whose peaks stand up like the tongues of a flame. A mounted official reins in at the stone where your shadow ends, gets down, and walks. So does the next.

choices.text: Turn your face to the Fire Mountain and keep it there

effects.log: Faces south, as the old ones lay. The mountain does not move, and neither do you. By evening the guards have stopped staring at you and started staring where you stare.

choices.text: Lie facing the gate instead, to watch who goes in

effects.log: You learn the faces of the court in a month: who looks at the ground, who looks at you, who looks at nobody. But all month there is a heat on the back of your neck like a hand, and it is coming from the south.

choices.text: Walk the dismount line first, nose to every stone where the horses must stop

effects.log: Twelve paces of road, every stone sniffed. A haechi that knows exactly where the line is will know exactly who crosses it mounted. Then you lie down, face to the south, and the Fire Watch begins.

events.text: An old minister of the Council does not dismount. He comes up the broad road in a palanquin under a green parasol, eight bearers at a trot, and passes your stone without slowing. His steward runs alongside with his hands folded and calls to the guards, to you, to the air: "His Excellency's knee! His Excellency cannot bend his knee!"

choices.text: "His knee." (the horn: true) Lay your ears back and let the palanquin by

effects.log: The horn is cold and quiet: the knee is real, swollen like a gourd. The next morning the old man gets out of the palanquin at the line anyway, and walks the twelve paces leaning on his steward, and bows to you at the end of them. Nobody has ever made him do anything. That is why he does it.

choices.text: Stand up in the road. Knee or no knee, the line is the line

effects.log: The bearers stop dead. The old man climbs down, white with pain, and walks past you in a silence that the whole gate hears. The line is kept. You feel, all day, a little smaller than you did, and you cannot say why.

choices.text: Let it pass, and watch where the palanquin goes

effects.log: Not to the council hall. Round the side of the palace, to the gate of the granary office, where the palanquin stays a long time. A knee can be true, and the road it is carried along can be another matter.

events.text: The old minister comes back alone at midnight, on foot, with a lantern and a box of persimmon cakes. He sets the box on your stone and sits on the step below it, rubbing his knee. "I will tell you why I do not dismount," he says. "If I get down in front of you, I must stop lying. I cannot afford to stop yet. Three more years. Eat a cake. They are very good."

choices.text: Push the box back down the step with your nose

effects.log: He sighs and takes it home. At the corner he stops and says, without turning round, "I did not think you would. I had to know." You did not know either, until the box was moving.

choices.text: Tell him: every time he passes, he must say one true thing aloud

effects.log: He laughs, and then he does it. "I am afraid of my son." "The granary is short by four hundred sacks." "My knee is the least of what is wrong with me." Three years of one true sentence a morning, and in the third year he dismounts and goes to the king with the granary books himself.

choices.text: Eat a cake. Three years is not so long

effects.log: Honey, dried persimmon, pine nuts. It is the best thing you have ever tasted, and in the morning your horn is cloudy as dishwater. Somewhere in the granary office, three more years of something begin. (A bribe: -8 Clarity)

events.text: A nursemaid brings three small children of some great house to look at you, and tells them in a carrying voice that the stone beast before the gate eats children who lie. The youngest, perhaps five, walks right up to your stone with both fists clenched and says: "I broke the inkstone. Not the cat." Then the child waits.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to the child

effects.log: The child stares, then turns round and announces to the nursemaid that the haechi bowed. The nursemaid says that is because the haechi was going to eat the cat. The cat, at home, is entirely blameless and is never told.

choices.text: Shake your head, so the horn rings, very softly

effects.log: A sound like ice on a spring. The child has never heard anything so beautiful, and goes home and confesses three more things to see if it happens again. It does not. It only rings for the first one.

choices.text: Say, gravely: "Nobody has ever been eaten for the truth"

effects.log: The nursemaid goes white: it speaks. The children are delighted: it speaks. By the next morning half the great houses of the capital have heard what the beast before the gate eats, and what it does not.

events.text: Thirty years without moving. There is moss in the curls of your mane and a wren's nest in the crook of your tail. Every dawn, the same family of gatekeepers brings a bowl of well water and sets it at your forefeet. First the grandfather, then the father, now {npc}, a grandchild with the family's flat ears, who talks to you the whole time as if you were a mule.

choices.text: Drink the water while {npc} is still there to see it

effects.log: {npc} stops in the middle of a long complaint about a cousin and watches you drink. "Grandfather said you never once did that while anyone watched," {he} says. "Thirty years." You did not know {he} had been counting for the whole family.

choices.text: Ask {npc} a question, after thirty years of listening

effects.log: You ask about the cousin. {npc} drops the bowl. Afterwards {he} tells you everything about the cousin, at length, every morning, for a decade, and none of it is a lie. It is the least tiring company you have had in a century.

choices.text: Shake off the moss and let the wren keep the tail

effects.log: The moss goes everywhere, the wren stays. {npc} sweeps up the moss without a word and keeps a piece of it in a box, for the family.

events.text: The old gatekeeper, {npc}, is dying, and has had {him} carried to the gate on a door so as to do it in front of you. {He} beckons you close. "In all the years of bringing you water," {he} says, "did I ever lie to you? Tell me true. I want to know before I go."

choices.text: "Once. You said the water was fresh, and it was yesterday's"

effects.log: There is a silence, and then {npc} laughs until {he} coughs. "The well froze," {he} says. "I was ashamed." {He} dies that night, still smiling, having been caught exactly once, in all those years, by the only witness who mattered.

choices.text: "Never"

effects.log: It is a kind lie, and it goes into you like a stone into a well. {npc} closes {his} eyes, content. Your horn aches all winter, as if someone had pressed a thumb into it. (-6 Clarity)

choices.text: "Ask me something you really want to know"

effects.log: {npc} thinks for a long time. "Was my father a good man?" {he} asks at last. You tell the truth, which is: mostly. It is enough. {He} dies at dawn with the water bowl beside {him}, filled.

events.text: The regent is rebuilding the palace, and wants stone guardians before its gate, and sends a carver, {npc}: a painter until {his} eyes grew too slow for colour, now a cutter of granite. {He} sits on a block in front of you with a string, a stick of charcoal and a great deal of patience, and starts to measure your brow.

choices.text: Sit as still as you can for {him}

effects.log: Forty days. {npc} talks to the granite more than to you, and to you more than to anyone else in the palace. On the fortieth day {he} says, "I have the ears." You feel a sliver of your sight go into the charcoal. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: Get up and walk away each time {he} sharpens the charcoal

effects.log: {npc} learns to sharpen very quickly. By the end of the season the drawings are of a beast getting up, and they are better than any drawing of a beast lying down, and {he} knows it.

choices.text: Let {him} put a hand on the horn, to learn its weight

effects.log: The hand is dry and careful. {npc} takes it away very quickly. "It is cold," {he} says. "Like a well in summer." The carver does not sleep that night, and nor, for some reason, do you. (-1 Clarity)

events.text: The stone is roughed out in the yard: your mane, your curled tail, your ears laid flat, your teeth, which {npc} has made a little friendlier than they are. Only the brow is still a block. "The horn," {npc} says. "The regent wants a lion that frightens people. A horn is thin. If it breaks in the cutting, the whole stone is ruined. I could leave a smooth brow, and nobody would ever know."

choices.text: "Cut the horn. A haechi without a horn is a lion"

effects.log: Three weeks on the horn alone, with the finest chisel {npc} owns. It does not break. When it is done the stone looks at you with something like your own sight, and a little more of it goes out of you into the granite. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: "Leave the brow smooth. Keep my sight where it is"

effects.log: A smooth brow, a good strong lion, nothing of you in it but the ears. {npc} is relieved and a little sad. Two hundred years from now nobody will remember that the beasts before the gate ever had horns. You will.

choices.text: "You are the carver. You decide"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time and then picks up the fine chisel. "Then it is a horn," {he} says, "and if it breaks, I break with it." It does not break. Neither does {he}.

events.text: An old official of the Office of Records comes to the stoneyard, leaning on a stick, to look at the carving. Then he turns and looks at you. "I have read every document in the archive," he says, "and none of them says a haechi stops fire. The old law says only that officials dismount where the haechi stands. The fire is a story the people tell. I thought someone should say so to your face."

choices.text: (the horn: true) Lay your ears back and bow to the old man

effects.log: The horn is cold and clean: every word true. You bow, as to the upright. He blinks. "Then why do you face the mountain?" he asks. "Because the people tell the story," you say, "and a story told by enough people is dry wood or wet wood. I would rather it was wet." He thinks about that all the way home.

choices.text: "Then I will be the document"

effects.log: He laughs, a dry little cough of a laugh. "Good," he says. "Somebody should be." He goes back to the archive and writes one line in the margin of the stoneyard accounts, in very small characters, which nobody will read for three hundred years.

choices.text: Lower your horn at him for his insolence

effects.log: He is not insolent. He is right, and old, and alone. He sits down hard in the stone dust, and something in your horn cracks very quietly as he does. You knew. That is the worst of it. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: They set the stone before the gate on a cold morning with a hundred men and ropes: your twin, granite, faces south beside your platform. That night, when the guards are asleep, you look across at it, and it seems to you, for a moment, that it looks back.

choices.text: Lie closer to it, flank to stone

effects.log: It is cold all night and warm by dawn. Two faces to the south now, one that breathes and one that does not. The Fire Mountain, if mountains notice, notices.

choices.text: Stare it down until you are sure it is only stone

effects.log: It is only stone. But it is cut to your measure, and when a liar passes the gate at noon you feel the granite twin lean toward them too, a half-breath after you.

choices.text: Shake your head so the horn rings, and listen for an answer

effects.log: Nothing. And then, so faint you might have dreamed it, a click in the granite, like ice on a spring. The guards say the next morning that a crack has appeared in the stone. The carver comes and looks and says it is not a crack, it is a vein, and goes away smiling.

events.text: {npc} the carver is very old now, and blind in one eye from granite dust. {He} is led to the gate by a grandchild and stands with a hand on the stone twin. "Did I get you right?" {he} asks you. "Tell me true. I have cut a hundred lions. You are the only one I ever met."

choices.text: "The ears, exactly. The teeth, kinder than mine"

effects.log: {npc} laughs and pats the granite. "I liked you better that way," {he} says. {He} dies before the first snow. The grandchild comes every year to sweep the stone twin, and talks to it, and sometimes to you.

choices.text: "You got the part of me that sees. That is the part that matters"

effects.log: A sliver more of your sight goes into the stone as you say it, freely given. {npc} feels it under {his} hand and stands there a long time. {He} dies that winter, and is buried, at {his} own wish, facing south.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let {him} feel the horn once more

effects.log: Cold, like a well in summer. {npc} nods as if {he} has been answered in full. Perhaps {he} has. {He} goes home and does not wake.

events.text: Your first night of the Fire Watch. The city sleeps; you do not. Across the river the mountain shaped like flame stands up against the stars, and after midnight you see what the old stories say: in the cracks of its rocks, very faint, a red glow, as if a kiln were banked inside. Something in there is awake, and has noticed that something on this side is awake too.

choices.text: Stare it down until dawn without blinking

effects.log: The glow fades at first light. You do not. A guard brings your water bowl at dawn and finds you still staring, and tells the barracks that the haechi won the first night.

choices.text: Count the peaks, and learn which one smokes first

effects.log: Seven peaks. It is the third from the east that smokes before the others, a thin grey thread on still nights. Whatever lives in the mountain breathes out through that one. You will watch the third peak for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Go down to the river at midnight and drink, to keep the horn cool

effects.log: The river is cold and full of the mountain's reflection. You drink the reflection. It tastes faintly of ash, which is not a good sign, and you come back to the gate with a clean horn and a thoughtful stomach.

events.text: A hot night with a south wind. A spark comes over the river: not a cinder but a little walking flame the size of a cat, with a face in it like a rotten persimmon. It hops from roof to roof toward the east market, sniffing at the thatch. When it sees you coming up the street it stops and says, very politely, "The Bird of the South sent me. Take it up with the bird."

choices.text: "The bird did not." (the horn: a lie) Lower your head at it

effects.log: The horn goes cold as a winter well. You lower your head and the little flame goes over the canal wall in a long hiss of steam. The fire demon sends its scouts with a lie ready. You will remember that the next time a fire blames the south.

choices.text: Stamp it out on the roof before it catches

ok.log: One great forefoot, a hiss, a smell of burned hair which is yours. The roof does not catch. The family under it never wakes.

fail.log: It dodges, and you put your foot through the thatch, and it is out over the next three roofs before you get your leg back. In the end you drown it in a dye-vat. The dyer is not grateful. (-10 health)

choices.text: Ask it, very quietly, who it really is

effects.log: It considers you. "A sniff," it says. "A taste. He wants to know which houses are dry." Then it goes out like a pinched wick. You do not need to ask who "he" is. You can see the third peak from here.

events.text: A breathless night in the dog days. The mountain speaks, in a voice like the roar inside a kiln door. "Every house in your city has a lie under its floor," it says. "A moved boundary stone. A false ledger. A child nobody explains. I only go where I am invited, beast. Every lie is an invitation."

choices.text: "Then I will take the invitations away, one by one"

effects.log: The mountain laughs: a rumble you feel in your forefeet. "There are a hundred thousand," it says. "Then I had better start," you say, and look away from it for the first time, down at the city, which is where the work is.

choices.text: "Name three houses." (the horn reads each name as it comes)

effects.log: It names three. The horn goes cold at two: a salt merchant, a court lady. At the third, a widow's house by the West Gate, the horn stays warm. The fire demon lies even about lies. You go to the two houses. You do not go to the third.

choices.text: Refuse to answer a mountain

effects.log: You put your chin on your forepaws and look at it as if it were a hill. After a while the voice stops. Whatever it wanted, it wanted a conversation, and you have given it nothing to burn.

events.text: On the main peak of the Fire Mountain, the monks of a little hermitage keep nine water jars with fire charms pasted on their lids, to hold the mountain's heat down. You go up one night to look. Eight jars are full. The ninth is dry, and the monk who keeps it swears by the Buddha that it was full at dusk and the mountain drank it.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Lower your head at the monk, very gently

effects.log: He sits down in the dust and confesses: he has been selling the charmed water as medicine in the villages below, a gourd at a time. You make him carry water up the peak until all nine jars brim. It takes him a month. The third peak smokes less that autumn.

choices.text: Carry water up yourself, a mouthful at a time, until the ninth jar is full

effects.log: All night, up and down the scree, your mouth full of spring water. At dawn the ninth jar brims. The monk watches the whole time with a face like a dropped plate, and in the morning he goes down the mountain and does not come back. (-8 health)

choices.text: Believe him. Mountains do drink

ok.log: And perhaps they do: the next morning the jar is full again, and the monk weeps. You never learn whether a mountain drank it, or a monk refilled it in the night, ashamed. You decide it does not matter which.

fail.log: The jar stays dry, and the next jar is dry by spring. The monk was lying, and you let the lie stand on the summit of the Fire Mountain, which is the worst place in the world to leave one.

events.text: A drought year. The paddies crack; the river shows its stones. The court closes the South Gate, because the south is fire, and opens the North Gate to call the rain. A royal envoy rides out to the great well dug on the next mountain, to pour offerings in it. All summer the third peak of the Fire Mountain smokes in daylight.

choices.text: Lie all summer in the shut gateway of the South Gate, between the city and the mountain

effects.log: The gate is shut and you are inside it, a door with a horn. The stones are hot enough to cook on by noon. You do not move. The smoke on the third peak thins and thickens, thins and thickens, like something breathing against a wall.

choices.text: Go with the envoy to the great well, and drink from it first

effects.log: The envoy is appalled; the well water is very good. When the offerings go in, you notice that the envoy's steward has kept back half the silk. You say nothing. It is a drought. You will say it after the rain.

choices.text: Tell the court the truth: closing the gate will not stop a fire. Clean granaries will

effects.log: The ministers are offended and the king is interested. Four granary clerks are found with false books that summer. The South Gate stays shut anyway, because a city likes its stories, and you do not argue with the story, only with the clerks.

events.text: You have swallowed fire now, and the mountain knows. One windless midnight it speaks again, but not in the kiln voice. This one is almost courteous. "Fire-eater," it says. "Come up. Not to fight. I have never had a guest who could eat what I am. I am curious what you taste like from the inside."

choices.text: "Not yet"

effects.log: "Not yet," the mountain repeats. "That is the first time anyone has told me not yet. Everyone else says never." The third peak smokes all night, thoughtfully. The invitation stands. You know it will be there when you are ready.

choices.text: "One day. And I will come to put you out"

effects.log: The mountain laughs, and the laugh shakes a tile off the gate tower. "Good," it says. "Then we each know what the other is for." It is the most honest thing anyone has said to you in the capital this year.

choices.text: Climb partway tonight, and swallow what you can of its slopes

ok.log: Halfway up, among red rocks, you swallow a river of heat in three breaths and come down at dawn with your belly glowing. The mountain says nothing. It is, you think, impressed. (-14 health)

fail.log: The smoke drives you back at the first ridge, your eyes streaming, your horn black with soot. "Not yet," the mountain says, kindly, which is worse than anything it could have shouted. (-20 health)

events.text: You walk down to the South Gate to see the old defences for yourself. Its name plaque is hung on end, not across, like a flame turned to face a flame; they say a prince wrote it so. Before the gate is a square pond full of lotus, dug, the gate guards tell you, so that the fire of the mountain sees water before it sees the city. Plaque, pond, and a beast before the palace: three walls against one mountain.
events.arc: The Pond at the South Gate

choices.text: Drink from the pond, slowly, where the guards can see

effects.log: Green water, lotus roots, frogs who disapprove. The guards tell everyone that the haechi blessed the pond. You did not bless it. You were thirsty. Both of these things become true.

choices.text: Stand under the plaque and read it upward

effects.log: The characters climb like smoke. Whoever wrote them knew what they were doing: an argument with a mountain, in ink. You find you respect the prince, whoever he was, more than most of the living.

choices.text: Count how many people throw rubbish in the pond

effects.log: Eleven before noon: fish heads, a broken sandal, a dead cat. A defence nobody tends is only a hole in the ground with a story attached. You lie by the pond all afternoon and nobody throws anything in it after that.

events.text: A minister of the Board of Taxation proposes to fill in the pond at the South Gate and build a storehouse for tax rice on the ground. In council he says the pond breeds summer fevers, that the old story about the mountain is a superstition, and that the storehouse will be built at no profit to anyone. The council looks at you, lying at the bottom of the steps.
events.arc: The Pond at the South Gate

choices.text: (the horn: a lie, the third part) Lower your head at him before the council

effects.log: The fevers might be true; the superstition might be true. "No profit to anyone" is a lie so cold your horn aches: the contract for the storehouse goes to his wife's brother. The council keeps the pond. The minister keeps his post, barely, and never comes up the road past you again.

choices.text: The horn is a fog. Argue for the pond anyway

ok.log: You do not know who is lying, so you argue for water. The old ministers like the sound of a beast defending a story older than they are. The pond stays.

fail.log: You cannot tell which part is false, and it shows. They fill the pond in the autumn, with carts of earth and the dead cat. The storehouse goes up in the spring, very fast.

choices.text: Argue for the pond as a story worth keeping

ok.log: "A city defended by water it can see sleeps better," you say, "and a city that sleeps does not knock over lamps." It is not the truth they asked for, but it is a truth, and it carries.

fail.log: The council is polite and unconvinced. They fill the pond that autumn. You stand on the new earth where it was, and the mountain across the river seems, to you, a little closer.

choices.text: Lower the horn and let the council decide without you

effects.log: It is their city. They fill the pond. You were sure enough that something was wrong, and not sure enough to say it in front of the king, and that is a kind of dry wood too.

events.text: The first dry spring after they filled the pond, the new rice storehouse on its ground catches fire in the night. You know, as you run down the road, exactly whose storehouse it is, and exactly whose brother-in-law built it, and that half the sacks in it are sand. Behind it are the houses of the porters who carry the rice.
events.arc: The Pond at the South Gate

choices.text: Pull the burning eaves down with your teeth before the porters' roofs catch

effects.log: The storehouse burns to the ground and nothing else does. In the ash the morning shows rows of sacks of sand. The minister is dismissed by noon. You did not let the fire judge him. The ash did that on its own. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let it burn. You know what is in it

effects.log: It burns, and the porters' houses with it, because fire has never once in its life stopped at the edge of the guilty. A haechi does not let fire judge. You did. The horn tells you so all winter. (-10 Clarity)

choices.text: Ring the bell, and wake the porters' lane before you run

effects.log: The bell at your throat goes off like a gong, and the porters' lane is out in the street in its sleeping clothes before the first spark crosses the alley. The storehouse burns alone. In its ash the sand shows. Everyone is up early enough to see it.

events.text: The lantern festival on the Buddha's birthday. The children of the South Gate quarter float paper boats with candles in them across the pond you kept, and the lotus has never been thicker. A small girl pushes her boat out too hard and it sails straight across to where you lie on the far bank, and stops against your forefoot.
events.arc: The Pond at the South Gate

choices.text: Push it back across with your nose, candle still burning

effects.log: A beast with a horn, nudging a paper boat across a pond in the dark, so carefully that the candle does not even lean. The whole quarter watches. Next year every child aims for you.

choices.text: Let it rest there and burn down against your foot

effects.log: It burns down to nothing against your scales and goes out in the water with a little sigh. The girl is satisfied: the beast has her wish now. You do not know what she wished. You keep it anyway.

events.text: At every corner of the great halls stands a broad bronze jar of water, wide as a cartwheel, with rings for handles. Palace servants keep them full. The cooks tell you why: the fire demon is so ugly that when it leans over the jar and sees its own face in the water, it runs. In winter, they add, they light a little fire under each jar so the water will not freeze. Fire guarding water guarding against fire. Nobody in the palace finds this funny but you.

choices.text: Look in a jar yourself, to see what the demon sees

effects.log: A grey-white face, a horn like a candle, eyes very clear. You are not ugly. You are not beautiful either. You look like something that sees, which, if you were a fire demon, would be the worst face of all.

choices.text: Go round every jar at dawn and check which are full

effects.log: Thirty-one jars full. The thirty-second, at the back corner of the queen's hall, is dry to the bronze, and has been, by the green line round its belly, for months.

choices.text: Drink from one, which scandalises the cooks

effects.log: Old bronze and rainwater. The cooks shriek and then giggle and then, very quietly, the eldest of them refills the jar from her own bucket and bows to it. You have made a ritual. You did not mean to.

events.text: The dry jar at the corner of the queen's hall. The palace eunuch whose duty it is to keep it full is fat, polite and very frightened of you. "It is full every morning, honoured beast," he says. "Every morning. The heat drinks it."

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Lower your head at the eunuch

effects.log: He confesses before your horn has stopped moving: he has been sending the water-carrier to his own household instead, every morning, for a year. The jar is full by noon. He is put to carrying the water himself, which, from the look of him, may save his life.

choices.text: (the horn, faint through the crack: a lie) Look at him until he speaks

effects.log: The mark is faint, as everything is through the crack, but it is there and it is true. You only look. He breaks in the time it takes a cloud to cross the sun. The jar is full by noon.

choices.text: Fill the jar yourself, a mouthful at a time, while he watches

effects.log: Sixty trips to the well. By the thirtieth, the eunuch is carrying buckets beside you, weeping, and by the sixtieth he has told you everything without being asked. (-5 health)

choices.text: Lower the horn. A dry jar is a small thing

effects.log: It is a small thing. So is a spark. The jar stays dry, the eunuch stays frightened, and the back corner of the queen's hall stays the one place in the palace where a demon could lean over and see nothing at all.

events.text: A hot night. Something comes over the palace wall: a little walking flame with a face like a split chestnut, looking for the halls. It goes round the jars at a crouching run, eyes shut, so as not to see itself. You catch it by the scruff at the corner of the throne hall, where it squeals like a kettle.

choices.text: Hold it over the water and make it look

ok.log: It opens one eye, sees, and screams so loud the guards wake on the far wall. It goes out over the palace roofs like a falling star going the wrong way. The halls do not burn for years. The cooks swear the jars did it, and you let them.

fail.log: It squirms, burns your lip, and drops out of your jaws into the dry grass behind the hall, where you spend the rest of the night stamping on it. Nothing big burns. You smell of singed mane for a month. (-12 health)

choices.text: "You are not as ugly as you think." Let it look on its own

ok.log: It looks. It does not run. It sits on the rim of the jar and stares at itself for an hour, and then it says, "I am, though," and goes home over the wall, and is not seen in the palace again for a long time.

fail.log: It does not believe you, and is right not to. It wriggles free and goes off over the roofs, giggling, and you hear later that a storehouse in the east market lost its roof that night.

choices.text: Look into the water beside it, side by side

effects.log: Two faces in the moonlit water: a beast with a horn, a spark with a grin. "Which of us is uglier?" it asks. "The one who lies," you say. It thinks about this, then hops off the rim and walks back to its mountain, looking at its feet.

events.text: The fire demon comes back after many years, not to burn, but to sit on the rim of the jar at the throne hall's corner. "Your turn," it says. "Look. Tell me what you see, and do not lie, haechi. I will know. I always know when the water is lying."

choices.text: Look, and say exactly what you see

effects.log: A beast older than the halls, a bell at its throat, a little soot round the horn. "Soot," you say. "Too many fires swallowed, too many sweet cakes refused too slowly." The demon nods, disappointed: it had hoped for something worse.

choices.text: Look, and see the smoke in your own horn

effects.log: There is more smoke in the water than you thought: grey curling through the white like ink in milk. The demon watches you see it. "There," it says, quite gently. "Now you know what I see every time." It goes away, and you graze bitter leaves for a season.

choices.text: Refuse. A haechi looks at others

effects.log: The demon laughs until it gutters. "That," it says, "is what every judge says." It goes. You do not look into a jar again for years, and when you do, you are almost relieved.

events.text: You dream, in a long dry summer, that you are very small and very cold and lying at the bottom of a bronze jar at the corner of a hall, and that something red comes and leans over the rim, and you look up at it with a face it cannot bear. You wake with your mane wet, though there has been no rain.

choices.text: Go and lie beside the jars that night, and listen to the water

effects.log: Thirty-two jars, and every one of them, if you listen long enough, has a sound like breathing. You could go down into them, you think. Not yet. But a beast could.

choices.text: Put the dream away. You belong before the gate

effects.log: You go back to your stone and face the mountain. But on hot nights afterwards you catch yourself glancing at the corners of the halls, at the bronze glinting there, the way one glances at a door one has been told about.

events.text: The regent's carpenters are raising the throne hall again, after the fires. Word goes round the scaffolding that secret charms will be laid in the ridge beam: paper brushed with the character for water, and the character for dragon, and little silver hexagons, so that the hall is roofed in water against the mountain. The head carpenter comes down the ladder at dusk and tells the regent's steward, before witnesses: "All laid in. Every one."

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Lower your head at the head carpenter

effects.log: The papers are in the beam. The silver is not: it is in his sleeve, six little hexagons, which fall out on the stones when he flinches. The steward picks them up one by one and counts them aloud.

choices.text: Climb the scaffolding at midnight and look for yourself

ok.log: The scaffold creaks under you like a ship. In the beam's groove: three folded papers, smelling of fresh ink. No silver. You come down and lie at the foot of the ladder, and in the morning the head carpenter finds you there, and knows.

fail.log: A beast your size was not meant for scaffolds. A plank goes, and you go with it, and land in the sawdust with half the carpenters watching. Nobody will look in the beam now, least of all the man who knows what is missing. (-10 health)

choices.text: Trust him. A hall is a carpenter's, not a beast's

effects.log: The beam goes up with drums and a long prayer scroll. You are not sure, and you let it go up anyway. Somewhere in the ridge of the throne hall there is now a lie, very small, roofed in, and dry.

events.text: The head carpenter comes to your stone at night, alone. His hands shake. "My son owes a moneylender for a gambling-house debt," he says, "no, I will tell it true: for a cart and an ox he lost in a flood. Silver was the only thing I could reach. They will flog me to death. Tell me what to do."

choices.text: "Put it back yourself, tonight, and tell the steward in the morning"

effects.log: He goes up the ladder in the dark with the six hexagons in his mouth, like a beast. In the morning he tells the steward everything. The regent, who likes a man who confesses before he is caught, has him beaten ten strokes instead of a hundred, and pays the ox.

choices.text: Say nothing. A haechi points, it does not counsel

effects.log: He waits for an answer that does not come. In the morning the steward takes him. The silver goes back in the beam. Somewhere a son finds out what a cart and an ox cost.

choices.text: Lower the horn. Tell the steward the silver was found on the scaffold

effects.log: It is the first time you have ever helped a lie on its way. The silver goes back in the beam, the carpenter lives, the steward is glad not to have to flog anyone. Your horn feels like a stopped bell. (-5 Clarity)

events.text: The raising of the ridge beam. Drums, a long scroll of prayers sealed into the beam, a boat flag planted on the roof of the hall to pull the mountain's fire across the river like a sail pulls wind. The regent stands below in a robe the colour of plums. Halfway through the rite, he looks across the courtyard at you, and raises an eyebrow, as if asking: well?

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to the beam

effects.log: The regent nods once, satisfied, and the drums go on. You bowed to a beam. Whatever it holds, it will keep, as wood keeps everything, and you would know.

choices.text: Shake your head, so the horn rings over the courtyard

effects.log: A single clear note. Two hundred carpenters stop, mallets raised. The regent smiles, very thinly. Nobody in the palace ever cheats the regent's beams again, and nobody is quite sure why.

events.text: Many years on, a fire takes the eaves of the throne hall in a winter night. It runs along the rafters, and at the ridge beam it stops, smoulders, and dies, as if it had walked into a wall of water. In the morning the king asks you, before the court: "Was it the charms in the beam? Or was it you?"

choices.text: "The charms, and the man who put the silver back"

effects.log: The king sends to find the old carpenter. He has been dead ten years. His grandson gets a bolt of silk and a story, which in a family like that is worth more than the silk.

choices.text: "The charms in the beam. Whoever laid them"

effects.log: The king nods and sends a bolt of silk to the guild of carpenters, without a name on it. A fire that stops at a beam is worth thanking someone for, and he is a king who likes to thank someone.

choices.text: "I do not know. Neither does anyone"

effects.log: The court murmurs: a beast that admits it does not know. The king smiles for the first time that winter. "That," he says, "is why I asked you."

choices.text: "Me"

effects.log: It is not quite a lie. It is not quite the truth either, and your horn knows exactly how far from it you are. The king is pleased. The court is awed. Your horn is cloudy for a year. (-6 Clarity)

events.text: A spring of northwest wind. It blows for forty days, dry as a kiln's breath, and the city's thatch rattles like paper. The bell at the watch tower is rung twice for nothing. On the third peak of the Fire Mountain the smoke leans toward the city, every day, as if listening. Something is coming, and you have perhaps a month.

choices.text: Wake the watch tower guards and make them keep the night

effects.log: You lie at the foot of the watch tower at night, and the guards, who would rather sleep, do not. They hate you a little. You can live with it.

choices.text: Walk the poor quarters and soak the worst thatch with river water from your mane

effects.log: Up from the river, shake, up from the river, shake, roof after roof in the servants' quarter of the west. People come out and watch, then start carrying buckets beside you. (-6 health)

choices.text: Do not leave the gate. Stare the mountain down

effects.log: Forty days face to face with the third peak, both of you leaning into the wind. Whatever is coming, it will not come from the mountain. You are almost sure of it.

events.text: It comes from a servant's kitchen in the west of the city, in the middle of the forty-first night of wind, and not from the mountain at all. By the time the watch bell rings, three lanes are burning. By the time you reach the bridge, thirty. A runner from the palace catches you there: the queen's order. Save the ancestral shrine first. Behind you the servants' quarter is roaring like a furnace with the door open.

choices.text: Obey the order. Run to the shrine

effects.log: The shrine of the royal ancestors does not burn: you lie across its gate all night and the sparks die on your scales. Two thousand roofs burn instead, in the west, and the ash falls on the shrine roof like snow. (A great fire)

choices.text: Turn back to the servants' quarter, and drive the people to the river

ok.log: You go through the burning lanes like a battering ram, kicking doors, roaring, herding whole families to the water. At dawn the wind drops. Four hundred roofs are gone, not four thousand. The queen hears that you disobeyed, and says nothing at all. (-18 health)

fail.log: You save the people of eleven lanes. The fire takes the other two thousand roofs anyway. In the morning you lie in the ash of the west with your mane burned short, and nobody blames you, and that is worse. (A great fire, -25 health)

choices.text: Ring the bell from the bridge, so the whole city wakes at once

effects.log: One note, then another, then a third, from the middle of the bridge. The whole capital is in the streets in the time it takes to draw breath, and a city that is awake puts out a city that is burning. Three hundred roofs. The queen's shrine is not touched.

choices.text: Walk into the middle of it and swallow the fire, lane by lane

effects.log: You swallow the west of the city until your throat is a chimney. At dawn you are lying in the last burning lane with smoke coming out of your ears, and the fire is inside you instead of on the roofs. (-25 health)

events.text: In the ash, the city wants someone to blame. They have a servant woman, from the kitchen where it started: she is on her knees before the magistrate's yard with her hands tied. "I banked the fire," she says. "I swear it. I banked it." The crowd wants her hanged. A rice merchant two lanes over is lending the magistrate his own guards.

choices.text: (the horn: true, every word) Stand between her and the crowd

effects.log: She banked it. The horn is cold, not at her, but at the rice merchant: his drying kiln, which he was not allowed to have inside the walls, two lanes up the wind. The magistrate sees where your head is pointing. The rope goes on another neck, and the crowd, being a crowd, cheers just as loudly.

choices.text: (the horn, faint: she is not lying) Stand between her and the crowd

effects.log: Through the crack the mark is thin as a hair, but true. You stand in front of her until the magistrate asks why, and then it all comes out: the merchant's kiln, two lanes up the wind.

choices.text: Look at the burned lanes, not at her, and follow the wind

ok.log: The burn runs from the north-west, and the kitchen is south-east of the worst of it. Two lanes up the wind there is a heap of charcoal and broken kiln bricks in a rice merchant's yard. You lie down on it. That is enough.

fail.log: The ash tells you nothing you can trust. They take her away. Months later the truth comes out about the merchant's kiln, and she is released, and goes home with her hands still marked by the rope.

choices.text: Lower the horn. The magistrate will judge

effects.log: He judges. It does not go well for her. A city that hangs the wrong servant after a fire has learned nothing, and the merchant builds a bigger kiln.

events.text: The king comes to the gate himself, on foot, through ash that is still warm. He stands in front of your stone and asks the question the whole city is asking. "You face the mountain. The fire did not come from the mountain. What use are you, haechi?"

choices.text: "None, against a kiln someone hid. Every hidden thing is dry wood"

effects.log: The king listens. It is not what he came to hear, but it is something he can use. Within a year there is an order: no kilns within the walls, no forges in the thatch quarters, and a reward for anyone who reports one.

choices.text: Say nothing, and turn your face back to the mountain

effects.log: The king waits, then goes. The court calls it pride. It is not. You have no answer that does not sound like an excuse, and you have never yet said one.

choices.text: "Ask me again in ten years, when the roofs are tile"

effects.log: "Tile is expensive," says the king. "So is ash," you say. He laughs, despite everything, and goes back to the palace to argue with the Board of Works.

events.text: The king orders the city rebuilt in tile, with the tiles given cheap or free to the poor, and a gap left after every fifth house, and walls of earth between the palace halls. In the west quarter a landlord with nine houses in a row refuses to pull down the fifth. "My grandfather built it before any order," he swears.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Lie down in his fifth house until they pull it down around you

effects.log: His grandfather sold rope. The house is ten years old. They pull it down with you lying in the middle of it, and you get up out of the dust and shake, and the gap stays a gap for four hundred years.

choices.text: Argue it before the magistrate, with the fire still in everyone's nose

ok.log: The magistrate has lost a cousin in the fire. The fifth house comes down. The landlord keeps eight, and every one of them is tiled by autumn.

fail.log: The landlord knows the magistrate's wife. The fifth house stays. You walk past it every spring for a hundred years, and every spring it is still dry.

choices.text: Change the city yourself: lie before the Board of Works until the order has teeth

effects.log: Forty days on the Board of Works' steps. Then inspectors with measuring rods, and fines, and a register of every fifth house in the city. The landlord's house comes down with the rest. The capital of tile and gaps that grows from it does not burn whole again in your lifetime.

events.text: Thirty years after the great fire. An old woman comes up the broad road every spring with a basket of bitter chinaberry leaves from the hills and sets it before your stone. She was eight that night. She says a horned beast picked her up by the jacket and dropped her in the river, and she has never once in her life been so frightened or so grateful.

choices.text: Eat the leaves in front of her, every one

effects.log: Very bitter, very fresh. She watches you eat them with her hands folded. Every spring until she dies, a basket. Every spring, your horn a little clearer for it.

choices.text: Tell her you do not remember her. It is true

effects.log: She laughs. "Of course not," she says. "There were hundreds of us. I remember you." She comes back the next spring anyway, and the next.

events.text: After the great fire, the king founds a fire office: a watch tower with a bell on every hill, and a company of fifty men with twenty axes, fifteen iron hooks and five ropes of three-strand hemp, to pull burning houses down before the fire can jump. Its first captain, {npc}, comes to show you the yard on inspection day. "Every bucket full," {he} says, "every hook sharp. The king's silver well spent."

choices.text: (the horn: a lie, the buckets) Walk down the line and tip one over

effects.log: Sand. And the next, and the next: water on top, sand under it, the rest of the bucket money in a chest in {npc}'s house. The hooks are sharp, though. You will give {him} that.

choices.text: Walk the line slowly, sniffing each bucket

ok.log: Water smells of nothing. Sand under water smells of a riverbank. The seventh bucket smells of a riverbank, and so does the eighth, and {npc} begins, very slightly, to sweat.

fail.log: Every bucket smells of well water to you. {npc} beams and bows you out of the yard. It will be some years before anyone finds out that only the top hand-width of any bucket was ever water.

choices.text: Praise the hooks and the hemp, and leave the buckets alone

effects.log: An office is a new thing and a new thing needs praise. {npc} glows. The men stand straighter. You decide to come back on a day {he} is not expecting you.

events.text: The buckets full of sand. {npc}, the captain of the fire office, comes to your stone at dusk. "Fifty men," {he} says, "and the king pays for thirty. I put sand in the buckets so the inspectors would see full buckets, and I pay the other twenty from the bucket money. That is the truth. Now do what you like."

choices.text: (the horn: true) Go with {him} to the king, and stand beside {him} while {he} says it

effects.log: The horn says every word is true, and you stand beside {npc} as {he} says it to the throne. The king is angry for one breath and then pays for fifty men. The buckets are filled with water the next morning, and the office keeps {npc} as captain for years.

choices.text: Lower your head at {him} for the sand. Sand is a lie in a bucket

effects.log: It was a lie, even with a good reason under it. {npc} is dismissed. The new captain, a nephew of somebody, pays for thirty men and fills all the buckets. The twenty who are let go, you learn, were the best of them.

choices.text: Lower the horn, and tell nobody

effects.log: Fifty good men and sand in the buckets. You keep the secret, and the office keeps the men. But a bucket of sand is a bucket of sand on the night it is needed, and you know that too.

events.text: A fire in the market quarter, and the fire office's men come running with their hooks to pull down a house and make a break. There are two houses in the line: a widow's, which the captain points at, and a rich wine-seller's new wing beside it, which would make a better break. The wine-seller is standing in the street with his hands in his sleeves. "The widow's house is older," he says. "It will fall cleaner."

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Put yourself in front of the widow's door

effects.log: The hooks stop. The horn goes cold at the wine-seller, and then, more faintly, at the captain's sleeve, which is heavier than it was this morning. They pull down the new wing. The fire stops at the gap. The widow brings you a cup of barley tea, very hot, and you drink it.

choices.text: Pull the new wing down yourself before anyone can argue

ok.log: You set your shoulder to the corner post and the new wing comes down in a cloud of plaster. The fire stops at the gap. The wine-seller says a great many things, none of them in front of you.

fail.log: The new wing is better built than it looks. While you strain at it, the men pull down the widow's house as ordered, and the fire stops there anyway. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let the fire office do its work

effects.log: They pull down the widow's house. It falls very cleanly. The fire stops at the gap, the wine-seller's wing is saved, and somewhere in the captain's sleeve there is a little more silver than there was this morning.

events.text: The watch-tower boy of the southern hill has rung the fire bell three times this year for nothing: a cooking fire, a lantern, the moon. The fire office wants to dismiss him. He comes to your stone in tears. "I saw smoke every time," he says. "I swear I saw smoke."

choices.text: (the horn: true) Go and lie on the southern hill with him for a night

effects.log: He is telling the truth: he sees smoke. At midnight you see it too, a thin thread from the third peak of the Fire Mountain, leaning toward the city. The boy has the best eyes in the capital. The fire office keeps him, and puts him on the tower that faces south.

choices.text: Tell him a watchman who rings for nothing is worse than none

effects.log: He goes home. The next watchman never rings early, because he is afraid to. That is a different kind of danger, and you think about it, later, on dry nights.

choices.text: Teach him the difference between cooking smoke and the mountain's

effects.log: A winter of evenings at the foot of the tower. Cooking smoke rises and spreads; the mountain's leans. By spring he rings the bell once, at the right time, and the fire office men are on the roof before the thatch catches.

events.text: The fire office has grown. It has a banner now, and a seal, and a hall, and the men want your likeness on the banner: a horned beast with a bell, facing south. The old captain brings the embroiderer to the gate. "Let them carry you into the fires," the captain says, "and they will run toward them."

choices.text: Lend your likeness to the banner

effects.log: The embroiderer counts your scales for a week. The banner goes into its first fire the next spring at the head of fifty men, and they run toward it, and the fire goes out a street sooner than it would have. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: Refuse. Let them run toward fires for their own sake

effects.log: The captain is disappointed, then thoughtful. The banner they make instead is a bucket, very plain. Men run toward it anyway. It turns out they always would have.

events.text: All year there has been a lump in your throat, hard and cool, under the scales. In the spring it splits the scales open and shows itself: a bell, bronze-green, grown out of you the way a horn grows. When you breathe it hums. When you shake your head it rings, a single note so clear that a pigeon on the gate tower falls off.

choices.text: Ring it on purpose, once, at dawn, over the whole city

effects.log: The note goes out over the tiled roofs and comes back off the mountain. Every dog in the capital barks. In the third peak of the Fire Mountain, the smoke stops, just for a breath, as if something had heard its own name.

choices.text: Keep very still, and learn what makes it ring on its own

effects.log: It hums at smoke. It shivers when a lie is told within ten paces. It is perfectly silent when a child sings. You spend a whole season learning its moods, and at the end of it you understand that it understood you first.

choices.text: Listen to which officials flinch when it hums

effects.log: Three of them flinch every morning. You note their faces. You do not need the horn for these; the bell has done the reading for you, and it does not even need you to look.

events.text: The bell rings by itself for the first time at a lie, and it does it in the middle of the rice market. A weigher of grain is swearing to a widow that her sack weighs three measures, not four. The bell goes off at your throat like a dropped gong. Every head in the market turns: to you, then to the weigher.

choices.text: Walk over and put your nose on the scale

effects.log: There is a lump of lead under the pan. The weigher is out of the market by noon, and every other weigher in the capital checks his pans that night by lamplight, alone, carefully.

choices.text: Let the bell speak, and do nothing else

effects.log: You do not have to. The market does it for you: the scale is turned over, the lead found, the widow paid four measures. You learn something useful: a city that has heard a bell needs very little else.

events.text: A minister of the Board of Rites petitions the king to have your bell muffled with felt, for the dignity of the court, which cannot conduct its business with a bell going off every time someone is diplomatic. Half the council signs it. The other half watch you to see what you will do.

choices.text: Lie quietly through the debate, and let the bell ring at every lie in it

effects.log: It rings nineteen times in one morning. On the twentieth, the minister of Rites stops in the middle of a sentence, looks at you, looks at the king, and withdraws the petition. The bell is silent. Everybody notices.

choices.text: Agree to the felt, but only for the council hall

effects.log: A compromise: a felt sleeve for the hall, none for the gate, the market or the courts. The court is grateful. You are a little sad. A bell that can be wrapped is a bell that can be wrapped further.

choices.text: Ask the king whether he wants a court that is dignified or one that is honest

effects.log: The king, who is young, says honest. Then, after a pause, both. You say he may have one. He chooses, and the felt is never made, and the court learns to be diplomatic in shorter sentences.

events.text: Midnight, and the bell at your throat wakes you with a low steady hum, not a lie's sharp ring. Smoke. You lift your head and smell it: the paper-makers' lane by the stream, where the drying racks stand close as reeds.

choices.text: Ring it with all your breath until the lane wakes

effects.log: The lane is in the street with buckets before the first rack is properly alight. They lose a week's paper, and nothing else. The paper-makers send you a sheet of their best, which is no use to a beast, and which you keep anyway.

choices.text: Run to the lane first, and ring when you are sure

ok.log: You are there in fifty bounds, and you are sure, and the bell goes off in the middle of the lane like a gong in a cupboard. The paper-makers come out swearing and stay to fight the fire. One rack burns.

fail.log: By the time you are sure, the second row of racks has caught. You ring until your throat is raw. They save the houses, not the paper. (-8 health)

events.text: A young censor asks you, in the hearing of the whole gate, whether he looks well in his new hat: the black hat embroidered with your likeness. He does not. It is too big, and the embroidery has given you a squint. You open your mouth to say something kind, and the bell at your throat begins to shiver.

choices.text: Say the kind thing anyway, and let the bell ring at you

effects.log: "Very fine," you say, and the bell goes off at your own throat like a slapped pot. There is a terrible silence at the gate, and then the young censor laughs so hard he has to sit down. He wears the hat for years and tells this story at every banquet. (-2 Clarity)

choices.text: Say the true thing: it is too big, and I have a squint

effects.log: The bell is silent. The censor goes red, then laughs, then takes the hat to a better embroiderer. The squint is corrected. The hat is still too big. He decides that, in your presence, this is a lesson in humility.

choices.text: Say nothing at all

effects.log: The bell is silent, and so are you, and so, after a moment, is the censor, who understands everything and goes off to find a smaller hat.

events.text: The king sends for you at night. Not the hall of audience: a small room with a brazier and a low table, and on the table four names on a sheet of mulberry paper. Scholars of the Office of Special Advisers, who say in their memorials what the king does not like to hear. "They plot," the king says. "Lower your head at them before the court, and you will never want for anything. You will only have to lower your head."

choices.text: "I will hear them first"

effects.log: The king smiles the smile of a man who has been told yes slowly. "Of course," he says. "Hear them." You go out past the guards and feel, all the way to the gate, as if you had swallowed a stone.

choices.text: "I do not point at names on paper"

effects.log: The brazier pops. The king looks at you for a long time. "No," he says at last, "I suppose you do not." He rolls up the paper. That is not the end of it, and both of you know.

choices.text: Ring the bell once, there, in the little room

effects.log: The note fills the room and goes on filling it. The king's hand, on the paper, is shaking. "They plot," he says again, much more quietly, and the bell says it is a lie, and he hears it say so.

events.text: The four scholars are brought before you one by one in a side court, under guard. An old man who speaks of the rites. A middle-aged man with ink on his cuffs. A young one who cannot stop shaking. A fourth who is very calm, and says, as the others did: "I have never plotted against the throne."

choices.text: (the horn: true, true, true, and a lie) Lower your head at the fourth alone

effects.log: Three men who say unwelcome things to the king are not three plotters. The fourth, calm, has been writing letters to a prince of the blood, and the letters are in his house, under the floor. You give the king one name, and it is not the name he wanted.

choices.text: The horn is a fog. Say you cannot tell, and will not guess

effects.log: Four faces, and the horn tells you nothing about any of them. You say so. The court gasps: a haechi that will not point. It is the most honest sentence you have spoken in years, and the king hates it.

choices.text: Lower your head at none of them, before the whole court

effects.log: You lie down in the middle of the side court with your horn on the flagstones. The four go home that night. The king does not speak to you for a year, and his huntsmen start, quietly, to learn your hours.

choices.text: Point at all four, as the king wishes

effects.log: You lower your head four times. Three of those times something in your horn cracks, and the cracks run together into one long crack, as if the horn could only bear one. Four warrants go out that night with your image on the seal. (A crack: -12 Clarity)

events.text: The king's anger is patient. A new stone haechi is carved for the gate, without a horn, without ears laid back, a fierce lion with its mouth open, and set on the other side of the road. The court is told the old beast grows old. Royal huntsmen are seen on the hills behind the palace at dusk, measuring the ground with their eyes.

choices.text: Stay on your stone. Let them see you are not leaving

effects.log: A beast before the gate, a lion across the road. The city chooses. Every morning there are bitter leaves on your step and nothing on the lion's, and after a year the king stops pretending, and the huntsmen go back to deer.

choices.text: Go to the four scholars' houses at night and lie at their gates

effects.log: Nobody arrests a man with a haechi asleep across his doorstep. The scholars write their memorials by lamplight with you breathing outside, and the king reads every one, and hates them, and does not send the guard.

choices.text: Change the court: lie in the hall of audience until the king speaks to you

effects.log: Forty days in the hall of audience, in the middle of the floor, in everybody's way. On the forty-first the king says, without looking at you, "Very well." The lion across the road is quietly moved to a temple in the hills.

events.text: Warrants with your image on the seal go out to four provinces. The families of the scholars you pointed at are scattered: a widow selling her hairpins at the East Gate, a son sent to a salt farm. The king is very pleased with you. He sends a second sheet of mulberry paper, with nine names.

choices.text: Refuse the second sheet, and go and find the widow at the East Gate

effects.log: You lie down at the edge of her mat of hairpins and do not say anything, because there is nothing to say. She does not forgive you. She does not drive you off either. The king takes the second sheet back unread. (-8 health)

choices.text: Go to the king and say aloud that three of the four were honest

effects.log: The court is silent as a well. The king says, very softly, "You pointed at them yourself." "Yes," you say. "That is the lie I am taking back." The three are released from the salt farms by spring. You are not forgiven, by anyone, which is right.

choices.text: Lower your head at the nine as well. It is easier the second time

effects.log: It is easier. That is the worst thing you have ever learned about yourself. Nine warrants, your image on every seal, and in the history the court is writing, a beast that lowered its head at whoever the throne pointed to. (A crack: -12 Clarity)

events.text: The one scholar you pointed at, the calm one, is brought before the king with his letters to the prince. He does not deny them. "I wrote them," he says. "I would write them again. But the other three knew nothing, and the haechi knew it. Let it be written that the beast told the truth even when it was not the truth the king wanted."

choices.text: Say nothing about his punishment. A haechi does not sentence

effects.log: The king sentences him to exile on a southern island. You do not say a word, either way. It is not your word to say. The other three go back to their memorials, and to saying what the king does not like to hear, a little more quietly.

choices.text: Ask the king, once, for the man's life

effects.log: You have never asked for anything at the throne. The king is so surprised that he gives it to you. Exile, not death. The scholar bows to you on his way out, not to the king, and the king notices.

events.text: The king is old now, grey and frightened of his heir's friends. He sends for you one last time to the little room with the brazier. There is a sheet of mulberry paper on the table, and a seal beside it already cut: your image, ears flat, horn lowered. "Clear the way for my son," he says. "Let the warrant carry your face. Then rest."

choices.text: Refuse. Lie down with your horn on the paper until he takes it back

effects.log: The old king waits a long time. Then he pulls the paper out from under your horn and burns it in the brazier, and the seal after it. "My father had a haechi too," he says. "It said no to him as well. I had forgotten." He dies that winter. The heir is crowned without a purge.

choices.text: Ring the bell, so the king hears his own fear

effects.log: One note in the little room. The king's cup shakes in his hand, and he looks at it, and for the first time in years he understands who is lying in that room, and it is not his son's friends. He puts the seal in the brazier himself.

choices.text: Lower your head at the paper. Let the warrant carry your face

effects.log: You lower your head. The seal comes down. And again, and again, through four reigns and four purges, your image on every warrant, until nobody remembers that the beast before the gate ever chose what it pointed at.

events.text: The palace is half rebuilt, and in the dry autumn the inner quarters under construction burn: stacked pine, scaffolds, a finished wing. By morning the court has three explanations: the regent's enemies, a monk's curse, and the Bird of the South. You walk through the ash before anyone else is allowed in.

choices.text: Smell the ash, beam by beam

effects.log: Lamp oil, on the north side of the timber stacks, where no lamp has any reason to be. Somebody poured it. Somebody who knew where the guards stand.

choices.text: Go back to the gate and look at the mountain

effects.log: The third peak was clear all night. Nothing crossed the river. Whatever burned the palace came from inside the walls, and walked on two legs.

choices.text: Listen to the rumours, all of them, and let the horn sort them

effects.log: Every rumour is half a lie, and the horn aches by evening. But one thing comes up in every telling: a servant who was first on the scene with a bucket. Heroes are remembered. You remember him too.

events.text: A second fire in the rebuilding, two years after the first: a whole hall of the queen's quarters, roof and all. This time the regent arrests two servants of a family that opposes him, and their master's house is surrounded. The two are brought in chains to the gate, and the regent's steward asks you, for form's sake: "These two?"

choices.text: (the horn: they are telling the truth) Lie down across the chains

effects.log: Neither of them has ever been inside the palace walls. You lie down across the chains, and the steward, who knows exactly what that means, goes very pale and goes to tell the regent that the haechi has an opinion.

choices.text: Lower your head at neither, and say: look closer to the buckets

effects.log: The steward does not understand, but the regent does, when he is told. The two servants are released the next day. Nobody apologises to them. Nobody ever does.

choices.text: Let the regent's law take its course

effects.log: They are questioned in the old way. They confess, because people do. You lie on your stone and hear about it, and the horn is so cold for a week that you cannot sleep.

events.text: There is a ceremony. A palace servant, {npc}, is rewarded with a bolt of silk for being first at both fires with a bucket. {He} kneels at the foot of the steps and says, beaming: "Both times I saw the flames from my window, and ran." {His} window, you happen to know, faces the wrong way.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Lower your head at {him}, in front of the regent

effects.log: The silk falls off {his} arms. {He} confesses on {his} knees: both fires {he} set, both fires {he} was first at. A bucket hero is fed and praised and given silk, and the hero's family had nothing to eat.

choices.text: Watch {him} at night instead

ok.log: Three nights later, a lamp in the timber yard and a figure pouring oil. You lie down in front of {him} without a sound. {He} drops the lamp, and you put it out with one foot, and {he} sits down on the logs and weeps.

fail.log: You watch for a month and see nothing. {He} is clever, or lucky, or done. Years later another hall burns, and the first servant there with a bucket is a different one, and you wonder.

choices.text: Lower the horn. Let {him} have the silk

effects.log: {He} takes the silk home. Perhaps it is enough, and {he} will not need another fire. Perhaps. A lie rewarded in front of the whole court is the driest wood you know.

events.text: {npc}, the bucket hero who set the fires, kneels before the regent. {His} mother and two sisters kneel behind {him}. The regent is in a mood to make an example. Everyone looks at you, to see what the beast says should be done to {him}.

choices.text: Say nothing. A haechi points; it does not sentence

effects.log: You lie down and look at the mountain. The regent sentences {npc} to a frontier garrison for life, and the family to nothing, because a beast that will not speak of punishment makes a regent think about it twice.

choices.text: Say one true thing: the family had nothing to eat

effects.log: It is not a plea. It is a fact. The regent hears it as a fact, which is the only thing regents respect, and sends the family rice from the palace stores. {npc} goes to the frontier. {He} writes, once, years later, to the gate: a letter nobody can read to you, which the gatekeeper keeps.

events.text: Fifty years on, a hall in the palace burns again, and within a day the old rumour is back in the markets: the regent's enemies, the monk's curse, the Bird of the South. A teahouse storyteller near the gate is telling the story of the bucket hero, and getting it wrong.

choices.text: Lie outside the teahouse until the storyteller gets it right

effects.log: It takes the storyteller four tellings, and a good deal of sweating, but by the fifth the bucket hero sets the fires, and the audience gasps in the right place. The city remembers, for another fifty years, to look first at whoever comes first with a bucket.

choices.text: Go and smell the new ash yourself

effects.log: A lamp knocked over by a cat. Nobody to blame. You tell the court so, and the court, which wanted somebody to blame, is disappointed in you, and you find you do not mind at all.

events.text: A red dawn, redder than dawns are. Beyond the Fire Mountain the whole southern sky is the colour of a forge, and out of it, from very far away, comes a voice like a bamboo flute played by someone who has never been refused anything. "Haechi of the gate," it says, "every morning you glare at my direction. What have I done to you?" The Vermilion Bird of the south does not come any closer. It does not need to.

choices.text: "I glare at the mountain, not at you"

effects.log: The red light flickers: something enormous, considering. "The mountain," says the flute, "is in front of me. You can see how one might mistake it." The glow fades with the sunrise. You think you have been laughed at, gently, by the whole south.

choices.text: "The south is fire. I face fire. Do not take it personally"

effects.log: "Everything is personal," says the flute, "to a direction." But it does not sound offended. It sounds as if it has been waiting a thousand years for somebody to answer it plainly.

choices.text: Say nothing, and keep glaring

effects.log: The red light holds a long time, then goes. On your step there is a single scarlet feather, warm as a cup of tea. Whether it is a greeting or a warning, you cannot tell, and the horn will not say: it does not read birds.

events.text: A drought, and the court's astronomers have a remedy: the Bird of the South sends the fire, they say, so the South Gate must be shut, the southern markets closed, and the bird insulted at a rite with water thrown south. The chief astronomer turns to you before the king: "The haechi faces south. The haechi knows."

choices.text: Say before the court: the bird does not send the fire. The mountain does, and the lies under the roofs

effects.log: The astronomers lose a great deal of face. The southern markets stay open, which is a mercy in a drought. In the south, very far off, a red light flickers once at dawn, which you choose to take as thanks.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Lower your head at the chief astronomer

effects.log: He does not believe it himself. He has a cousin with a granary in the north quarter who would very much like the southern markets closed. The rite is cancelled. The cousin's rice sells at an ordinary price.

choices.text: Let the court have its rite

effects.log: Water is thrown south, with drums. The southern markets close. The poor of the south quarter go hungry in a drought for a story that is not true, and the red dawns that year are very red indeed.

events.text: A scarlet feather on your step at dawn, still warm, and with it the flute voice, very low, almost at your ear. "The thing in your mountain tells its sparks to say I sent them," it says. "I have heard it. I am a fire too, haechi, but I am not that one. Will you believe a bird, when your horn cannot read me?"

choices.text: "Yes. Your sparks have never once lied to me. His always do"

effects.log: There is a long, warm silence from the south. "No one has ever trusted me on the evidence before," the bird says. "Only on the beauty." The feather on your step stays warm all winter.

choices.text: "I will believe what I see. Show me"

effects.log: The next spark that comes off the mountain, you see a red light in the south flare at the same moment, as if something enormous had turned its head to watch. It does not come from the bird. It goes toward it, and dies on the way. That is enough.

events.text: The Bird of the South asks you a strange thing. "Turn your head," it says, "one night. Not at the mountain. At me. I want to be looked at by something that sees, once, without being blamed." The third peak of the Fire Mountain is quiet tonight. It is very rarely quiet.

choices.text: Turn your head for one night, and look

ok.log: You look south past the mountain all night, and the whole of the south looks back: a red light, and inside the red a shape you will not describe to anyone, and inside the shape something that has been blamed for a thousand years and is tired. The mountain sends nothing. The bird says, at dawn, "Thank you." It is the only time.

fail.log: You look, and it is worth it. But at midnight, while your face is turned, the third peak sends a thread of sparks over the river, and a stable in the south quarter burns. The bird sees it too. "I am sorry," it says. So are you. It was still worth it.

choices.text: "The watch is the watch. I cannot"

effects.log: "I know," says the bird. "That is why I asked you." It goes, and the red in the south fades to an ordinary dawn. You think about it for a hundred years. You would make the same answer.

choices.text: Look at its reflection in the river instead, with your face still to the mountain

effects.log: The river carries the red of the south past your feet all night, and you look down into it without lifting your eyes from the mountain's side of things. "That is cheating," says the bird, delighted. It is. It is also how a haechi looks at anything.

events.text: Hinges go missing from the gates of the capital. Then nails from the bridge. Then, one night, the doors of the western armoury are found bitten through, and a hundred spearheads are gone, and the shafts lie in a heap like chewed straws. The guards fired arrows at something huge in the dark. The arrows bounced. In the morning the city is whispering a name from the end of the last kingdom: the Iron-Eater.

choices.text: Follow the footprints out of the armoury

effects.log: Deep, heavy, splayed like a bear's and pressed into the earth as if something were carrying an anvil. They lead to the blacksmiths' quarter, and stop at a forge, and then there are no more tracks and no more anvil.

choices.text: Stay at the gate. The fire is your watch, not iron

effects.log: You keep your face to the mountain. But at night you hear it, very far off: a slow, contented crunching, like a horse eating sugar cane, somewhere among the forges.

events.text: The court sits in emergency. Arrows cannot kill the thing; swords break on it; it has eaten the iron chain off the palace well. An old sage from the mountains stands up and says it plainly: "It cannot be killed by iron. It can be killed by fire." Then every face in the hall turns to you, the beast that holds the fire back. "Let the mountain's fire through the gate for one night," says the chief minister, "and burn it."

choices.text: "No. Fire let in for one night does not leave in the morning"

effects.log: The court is furious, and frightened, which is the same thing in a hall of ministers. But nobody who has lived through a great fire argues for long. The sage nods at you, very slightly, as if you had passed something.

choices.text: (the horn: true, the sage) "Fire can kill it. That does not mean it should"

effects.log: The horn is cold and certain: the sage speaks the truth. Fire would kill it. You say so, so nobody can accuse you of hiding it. Then you ask the hall a question nobody has asked yet: why is a thing that eats iron in the one city of the land that is full of weapons?

choices.text: Agree. Let the fire through, once, under your eye

effects.log: You get up off your stone for the first time in years and turn your back on the mountain. The guards gasp. Across the river, on the third peak, something stirs that has been waiting a long time to be let in.

events.text: You find it at night in the blacksmiths' quarter, sitting in a cold forge and chewing an anvil the way a child chews a rice cake. It is large and lumpy and patient and covered in a hide like rusted plates. It swallows. "They say fire can kill me," it says, in a voice like a cart going over cobbles. "Is that true? You would know. They say you know."

choices.text: "It is true. Leave the city, and they will have no reason to try"

effects.log: It sits with that a long time, chewing slowly. Then it gets up, and the forge floor groans, and it walks out of the north gate before dawn, eating only the hinges on the way. It does not come back in your lifetime.

choices.text: "No." Lie, to keep it calm

effects.log: It believes you. It has never met a haechi before. It goes back to its anvil, content, and you walk back to the gate with your horn aching like a broken tooth. (-6 Clarity)

choices.text: Offer it the old rusted spears from the armoury, if it will leave after

effects.log: Rusted iron, it tells you, is the best: soft, red, with a taste of rain. You lead it to the old armoury, and it eats three hundred broken spears in a night, and leaves by the north road with a heavy, cheerful tread. The court is very angry about the spears.

events.text: They do it without you, or with you, it no longer matters. The court's men set fire to the thing's tail with pitch and torches, and it runs, red-hot, through the market quarter, screaming like a forge with the bellows broken, and everywhere it touches, the thatch catches. Behind it the iron it has eaten is pouring out onto the street: hinges, nails, spearheads, a palace well chain.

choices.text: Run ahead of it and drive it toward the river

ok.log: You meet it head on at the market cross and turn it with your shoulder, once, twice, and it goes into the river in a cloud of steam that hides the whole bridge. When the steam clears there is nothing left of it but iron on the riverbed. Two streets of thatch burned, not twenty. (-15 health)
