fail.log: It is faster than a thing that size should be. By the time you turn it into the river, half the market quarter is alight, and the wind is up. In the morning there is a heap of iron on the riverbed and a quarter of the city in ash. (A great fire, -25 health)

choices.text: Swallow the fire off its back as it runs

effects.log: You run beside it and swallow the burning pitch off its hide in long breaths, and it slows, and stops, and sits down in the street, cold and shaking and alive, with its iron all round it like a spilled purse. "Thank you," it says, absurdly. (-22 health)

choices.text: Ring the bell and get the market out of its path

effects.log: Nobody dies. That is what you chose. The thing burns itself out in the river at dawn, and the market quarter burns with it, and the court gives you no thanks at all. (A great fire)

events.text: Spring. The court collects the iron that came out of the thing, or was left behind by it, and has it melted down. The question is what to cast. The minister of War wants spearheads. The minister of Rites wants a bell for the watch tower. Someone remembers to ask the beast before the gate.

choices.text: "A bell for the watch tower"

effects.log: The iron of a thing that could not be killed becomes a bell that rings at fire. It has a strange note, low and rough, like a cart on cobbles. You like it very much.

choices.text: "Ploughshares. Give it back to the fields"

effects.log: The minister of War is outraged. The king, who is in a good mood, agrees. Three hundred villages get iron ploughs that spring, and the next time an Iron-Eater wanders down from the north, it will find a city with fewer spears in it.

choices.text: "Spears. They will need them"

effects.log: It is true, and it is sad. The armoury is restocked by summer, every head bright. You can smell the iron from the gate on still nights, and wonder what will come to eat it next.

events.text: The old gardener of the great pavilion's pond shows you something at low water: two dark bronze shapes in the mud among the lotus roots, long and coiled, sunk there long ago against fire. "The Azure Dragon," the gardener says, "or so my grandfather said. Two guardians against one fire, honoured beast. You and them."
events.arc: The Bronze Dragons in the Pond

choices.text: Lie by the pond and look at them a long time

effects.log: Bronze, green with age, not alive. And yet there is something in the water around them that is cooler than the rest of the pond, the way water is cooler where a spring comes up. Two guardians. You decide not to be jealous.

choices.text: Ask the gardener how much of the story is true

effects.log: The horn listens while he talks. Grandfather really did say it. Grandfather was, the horn adds, a great liar about almost everything else. But not about this, as far as the horn can tell. That is the most a horn can tell about a grandfather.

choices.text: "I know whose likeness that is." Lay your ears back to the bronze

effects.log: You do know. Another life, in another skin, went down into this pond and stayed. The bronze does not answer. The water around it ripples, once, though there is no wind, and the gardener drops his rake.

events.text: A summer fire in a hall beside the great pond: a lamp, a curtain, a gallery of dry cedar. It runs along the gallery toward the pavilion and stops dead at the water's edge, as if it had looked down. The next morning the court comes to thank you for it, with the king's own cup of honey wine. You were at the gate all night.
events.arc: The Bronze Dragons in the Pond

choices.text: "The pond did it. Thank the gardener, and what is under the water"

effects.log: The court is confused, then charmed. The gardener gets the king's cup. The pond gets a rite every summer after, with offerings floated over the place where the bronze lies. You think that is right.

choices.text: Accept the thanks. The court needs a guardian it can see

effects.log: You accept the honey wine and let it stand before you, untouched. The bowl is very fine. The court is reassured. Somewhere under the lotus the bronze lies in the mud and does not mind, and your horn, which minds, is cloudy for a season. (-4 Clarity)

choices.text: Say nothing either way

effects.log: The court decides you are being modest. The gardener knows better, and winks at you, and you are glad there is one person in the palace who saw the fire stop at the water.

events.text: A hot, still night. You leave the gate for an hour, which you almost never do, and lie at the edge of the great pond where the bronze is sunk. The water is cool against your flank. Something under it is keeping watch the same way you are, in the other direction.
events.arc: The Bronze Dragons in the Pond

choices.text: Stay until dawn, back to back with what is under the water

effects.log: You face south; the bronze, as far as you can tell, faces north. Between you the palace is held like a bowl in two hands. You go back to the gate at first light, and it is the best night's rest you have had in fifty years.

choices.text: Go back to the gate at once. You are not a beast who rests

effects.log: An hour is enough. You lie down on your stone again and face the mountain, and you are less alone than you were, and you do not tell anyone why.

events.text: A magpie lands on your stone with a message it plainly considers beneath it. The White Tiger of the right ridge, who keeps the Autumn Court on the rocky mountain west of the palace, asks you to sit beside it at the equinox, "as the one who sees the facts." It has never asked anyone for anything, the magpie adds. It has never asked for anything twice.

choices.text: Go up to the right ridge at the equinox

effects.log: You climb the rocky mountain in the first frost. The court is a granite ledge with a view of the whole capital, and the White Tiger is there before you, enormous and pale, its tail curled round its feet, looking at you exactly as you look at a liar: politely, and all the way through.

choices.text: Send the magpie back: the gate cannot be left

effects.log: The magpie looks at you as if you had refused the moon. It flies back west. That autumn the red maples on the right ridge are redder than usual, which may mean nothing.

choices.text: Go, but say you will see only one case

effects.log: The White Tiger hears the condition and its whiskers move: amusement, or approval, or both. "One," it says. "We will see whether you stay for the second."

events.text: The first case of the Autumn Court. A charcoal burner is dragged up the ridge by the villagers under it, accused of the mountain fire that burned their chestnut woods. He swears he banked his kiln. The White Tiger looks at you. "You see," it says. "I decide. Tell me what is."

choices.text: (the horn: true) "He banked it. The fire came from a lightning-struck pine"

effects.log: The tiger hears it, and looks at the villagers, and something in the set of its shoulders changes. The charcoal burner goes home. The tiger turns its head and looks at you for a long moment. "Useful," it says. From a tiger, that is a hymn.

choices.text: "I cannot read him clearly. Do not decide on my word"

effects.log: The tiger is silent a long time. Then it sends the villagers home to look at the burned trees again. "You admit what you do not see," it says. "Most witnesses would rather be wrong."

choices.text: Say what you think the sentence should be

effects.log: The tiger turns its whole head toward you, slowly. "That," it says, "is not what I asked." You have stepped across a line, and the frost on the ledge between you feels a little thicker all evening.

events.text: Another equinox, another case. A young woman stole a sack of rice from a landlord and lied about it under oath, and the horn is certain: she did it, and she lied. It is also certain why: a little brother, and the winter. The White Tiger leans toward severity. You disagree, once, aloud.

choices.text: "She is guilty, and the lie was for the child. Both are facts. Weigh both"

effects.log: The tiger growls, low, for a long time. Then it gives her a winter's labour in the landlord's house and the landlord a winter's obligation to feed the brother. "You are inconvenient," it tells you. It sounds almost fond.

choices.text: State the facts and lower the horn on the rest

effects.log: You say she stole and she lied, and you say nothing about the brother, because the tiger did not ask. It sentences her severely. Later, alone, you wonder whether the brother was a fact you were bound to say. You decide that he was.

events.text: Decades on, the magpie comes back to your stone, older and even more disdainful. "The White Tiger says," it recites, "that the Autumn Court has been very quiet since you stopped coming. It says it does not miss being disagreed with. It says to come at the equinox."

choices.text: Go, and disagree with it at least once

effects.log: You do. The tiger listens, growls, and changes one sentence out of nine. On the way down, you hear the magpie telling a crow that the two of them are as bad as each other, and you take it as a compliment.

choices.text: Send back: "The gate needs me. Tell it the truth is the same as last time"

effects.log: The magpie flies west, muttering. The tiger, you hear later, laughed, which nobody on the right ridge had heard it do for two hundred years.

events.text: A hall in the palace catches in the night, and you are there before the guards, and you do the thing that has been growing in you for a century. You open your mouth to the fire, and breathe in. It comes. It comes down your throat like boiling honey and lies in your belly like a coal, and the eaves above you go dark and smoking, and the guards, arriving with buckets, stop dead.

choices.text: Keep breathing it in until the last ember

effects.log: The whole eave, rafters and all, and then the curtain, and then a burning bird's nest. When it is done you sit down on the steps and cough a single spark that floats up over the hall like a lantern. (-15 health)

choices.text: Swallow just enough, and let the guards finish with water

effects.log: Half the fire, then the buckets. A good fire is a shared one, you decide, and the guards decide the same, and tell it in the barracks with themselves in it, which is fair. (-8 health)

events.text: The fire you swallowed does not go out. It sits in your belly all year like a banked kiln. You cough smoke in the mornings. In the coldest weeks of winter the children of the gate quarter come and stand in front of you with their hands held out to your mouth, as if you were a brazier.

choices.text: Breathe on their hands, very gently, every morning

effects.log: Warm, smoky breath, and twenty small pairs of hands. Their mothers are scandalised and then grateful. By spring the embers in you have burned low, and you are almost sorry.

choices.text: Go down to the river and lie in it until the embers die

effects.log: The river steams around you for a day and a night. The fishermen downstream say the water tasted of ash for a week. When you climb out the coal in your belly is grey and quiet.

events.text: North of the palace, under the white granite of the guardian mountain, there is a spring so cold it hurts the teeth. A hermit keeps it: an old man with a gourd and no opinions. When you come down to it with your belly full of smoke, he looks at you and moves his gourd out of the way.

choices.text: Lie in the spring all season, with only your horn above the water

effects.log: A season of cold so deep that your scales ache. The smoke goes out of your horn in grey threads, and the hermit sits beside you saying nothing, and by autumn your horn rings when you shake it, clear as it rang at the edge of the world.

choices.text: Drink, thank him, and go back to the gate

effects.log: One long drink, a bow, and back to the mountain. The hermit says, as you go, "Come back when it hurts." It is the only thing you ever hear him say.

events.text: Something is wrong with your tongue. You chew a chinaberry leaf and it tastes of nothing: not bitter, not sweet, only of ash. The fire has burned the taste out of you. And without the bitterness, you notice, the horn does not clear the way it used to.

choices.text: Eat the bitter leaf anyway, every day, taste or no taste

effects.log: It is like praying in a language you have forgotten. But the leaf does not need you to taste it to do its work. Slowly, over a year, the horn clears, and one spring morning the bitterness comes back all at once, and you nearly weep.

choices.text: Go up into the hills and find the bitterest tree there is

ok.log: An ancient chinaberry on a ledge above a gorge, so bitter that the goats will not go near it. Even your burned tongue can taste it. You come back to the gate with your eyes watering and your horn clean.

fail.log: Every tree in the hills tastes of ash to you. You come back no better, but a little calmer, which is something.

choices.text: Stop swallowing fire for a while, and let the tongue heal

effects.log: You ring, you watch, you swallow nothing. The city is a little drier for it. Your tongue heals in three years, and the first leaf you taste is so bitter you sneeze.

events.text: A drought year, the worst in living memory. The third peak of the Fire Mountain smokes by day and glows by night, and the glow is spreading down the slopes toward the river. The city is tinder from wall to wall. You know what must be done, and you know where.

choices.text: Climb the Fire Mountain and swallow its fire at the summit

ok.log: Up through red rocks and black smoke to the third peak, where the mountain opens like a kiln door. You swallow its fire in one long breath. You come down at dawn with embers in your belly, and behind you, for the first time in a hundred years, the Fire Mountain is cool. (-20 health)

fail.log: Halfway up, the smoke closes over you like water, and you swallow what you can on the slopes and come down coughing. The glow on the third peak shrinks a little. Not enough. Not yet. (-25 health)

choices.text: Ring the bell over the city every night of the drought instead

effects.log: Every night, one note. The city sleeps lightly all summer, and every lamp is watched, and every kiln is banked twice. Nothing burns. The mountain glows on, unswallowed, and waits for another year.

events.text: A salt merchant tells you, before the gate, that his salt is from the eastern sea and never touched with sand. It is an obvious lie: you can see the sand. And the horn says nothing. Nothing at all. You shake your head, and the horn rings like a cracked pot, and you realise you have not felt it go cold at a lie for a year.

choices.text: Admit it, at least to yourself: the horn is smoked

effects.log: Fires swallowed, smoke breathed, sweet things refused too slowly, a city thick with lies. The horn is grey at the root like an old pipe. A haechi who knows it cannot see is better than one who thinks it can.

choices.text: Lower your head at the merchant anyway. You can see the sand

effects.log: The sand is there, horn or no horn. The merchant is fined. But you know now that you judged him with your eyes, like a magistrate, and that the next liar will not be so careless.

events.text: There are four chinaberry trees inside the city walls, and you know them all. The minister of Public Works means to cut down the oldest of them for the new gate of his house: a fine timber, straight as a flute. It is the one you graze on hardest in the dry years.

choices.text: Lie under the tree until he gives up

effects.log: A month under the tree, chewing its leaves. The woodcutters go round you twice and go home. The minister finds his timber elsewhere, and grumbles to the king that the haechi has opinions about trees. The king says the haechi has opinions about everything.

choices.text: Change the city: have every chinaberry inside the walls put under the gate's protection

effects.log: You lie before the Board of Public Works until the order is written. Four trees, then, as the city learns why, forty: every ward plants one. In a hundred years the capital is full of bitter shade, and nobody quite remembers why.

choices.text: Let it go. Trees grow back. Find others in the hills

effects.log: The tree comes down, and is a very good gate. You go out to the hills for your bitter leaves, half a day there and half a day back, and the horn clears more slowly than it did.

events.text: A herb-woman from the southern hills starts leaving a basket of bitter chinaberry leaves on your step every week. She says she wants nothing for it. A minister's steward, who has seen her, tells you she is in his master's pay, and the leaves are a way to buy your goodwill.

choices.text: (the horn: the herb-woman true, the steward a lie) Keep eating the leaves

effects.log: The horn is clean enough again to read them both. She wants nothing. The steward wants you to refuse a gift and starve your horn, which is a very clever lie, and you are almost sorry to have caught it.

choices.text: The horn is a fog. Refuse the leaves, to be safe

effects.log: You turn the basket away. She does not come again. You will never know which of them was lying, and your horn, deprived of its best bitter leaves, stays clouded a year longer.

choices.text: Eat the leaves, and watch whether anyone asks a favour

effects.log: Nobody asks for anything, ever. Week after week she brings you five hundred baskets, and on the day she dies, her son brings the five hundred and first, and says she told him to.

events.text: A clean winter. No fires to swallow; no feasts; a cold north wind that blows the city's smoke out over the river. One morning you shake your head, and the horn rings: a clear note, ice on a spring. For a moment you are a kid again at the edge of the world.

choices.text: Sit the Stone Sleep for a whole season, to keep it clear

effects.log: Stone to the knees, snow on your mane, the horn ringing faintly every time the wind shifts. When you wake, the city has dried a little in your absence. The horn has not.

choices.text: Go straight to the council hall, and see what the clean horn shows you

effects.log: Two ministers you had trusted for twenty years. The clean horn finds them both before noon. A smoked horn is a merciful thing, you think, on the way back to the gate. You would not have it back.

events.text: A haechi comes down the north road one spring morning, grey-white and long in the leg, with a horn like a white candle and a scar on the brow that you put there yourself, a week of butting over nothing at the far spring, when you were both kids. The haechi of the far spring has come south. They walk up the broad road, ignoring the officials, and lie down on your stone beside you as if they had always lain there.
events.arc: The Haechi of the Far Spring

choices.text: Butt them, once, gently, for old times

effects.log: Brow to brow, horns crossed, a click like two icicles. The guards stare. Neither of you says anything for a whole day. You do not need to.

choices.text: "You came all this way"

effects.log: "Every quarrel on the frontier," they say, "was settled long ago. It got very quiet." They look at the city, and the river, and the mountain. "This is not quiet," they observe. You agree that it is not.

choices.text: Make room, and say nothing

effects.log: There is room. There always was, on that stone. You had not noticed, until now, that you had been lying on one side of it all this time.

events.text: The haechi of the far spring does not like the capital. The air is thick; the food is sweet; everybody lies, all the time, about everything, and their horn aches from it. "How do you stand it?" they ask, chewing a leaf and making a face. "It is like lying down in a smokehouse."
events.arc: The Haechi of the Far Spring

choices.text: "I do not stand it. I sit"

effects.log: They laugh, the first time since they came. Then they lie down a little closer, and that night the two of you stare the mountain down together, and the third peak, for once, does not smoke.

choices.text: Take them to the four chinaberry trees and the cold spring in the north

effects.log: You show them every bitter tree and clean spring in the city, and they show you that you had missed one, behind a temple, under a wall. Two horns clear faster than one.

choices.text: "Go home, if it hurts you"

effects.log: They look at you a long time. "You stand it," they say, "because nobody else would. That is a reason. It is not a happy one." They stay, for now.

events.text: In the hottest night of a dry summer the haechi of the far spring says what they have been carrying since they came. "There are two ways for us," they say. "A pair before this gate, facing the mountain, until we turn to stone and the city takes us for its sign. Or home: the spring at the edge of the world, kids with horns like candles, quarrels nobody ever hears of. I will not choose for you."
events.arc: The Haechi of the Far Spring

choices.text: "Stay. A pair before the gate"

effects.log: They nod slowly, as if you had said exactly what they feared and hoped. "Then I need a while," they say, "to learn to want it." You give them a while. You have plenty.

choices.text: "Not yet. Ask me again when the city is cooler"

effects.log: "The city will never be cool," they say. "That is why it needs us." But they agree to ask again, and lie down beside you, and do not sleep.

choices.text: "Home. I have been away long enough"

effects.log: They look at the city for a long time, and then at you. "You do not mean it yet," they say, gently. "But you will." The horn, which reads everyone but you, says nothing.

events.text: Years have passed since the haechi of the far spring asked. They do not ask again. They only lie beside you one morning with their face to the north instead of the south, and wait for you to notice, and you do.
events.arc: The Haechi of the Far Spring

choices.text: Turn your face south beside theirs: a pair before the gate

effects.log: They turn round, slowly, and lie down with their face to the mountain beside yours. Two faces to the south. The guards notice; the city notices; within a year the children of the capital are drawing two horned beasts, never one. When the time comes, the gate will have its pair.

choices.text: Turn your face north beside theirs: the clear spring

effects.log: You turn round on your stone, for the first time in centuries, and look north up the road toward the birches and the snow. You do not leave yet. But you both know now which way you will go when you do.

choices.text: Let them go home alone. The gate is yours

effects.log: They go at dawn, up the north road, without looking back, which is how you know how hard it was. The stone is too wide again. You lie in the middle of it, out of spite, and face the mountain.

events.text: The pair before the gate. The stone lions on the gate roof, and on your stone, the two of you, living. The city has started calling you the Pair, as if you were one thing. A child asks the haechi of the far spring, very seriously, which of you is the real one.
events.arc: The Haechi of the Far Spring

choices.text: Let them answer

effects.log: "Neither," they say. "We take turns." The child goes away entirely satisfied, and tells everyone, and the story outlives the both of you.

choices.text: Answer: "The stone one. We are only waiting to become it"

effects.log: It is true. The child looks at the stone lions on the gate roof, and at the two of you, and understands it better than you would like. Some children do.

events.text: A brewer of the capital, an old man with arms like oak roots, asks permission to dig under your stone. He has three jars of white wine, the best he has ever made, sealed with clay and pine resin. "To be opened in a hundred years," he says, "on a day when the whole land is glad. Who better to guard them than you?"

choices.text: Lift your forefeet, and let him dig

effects.log: He digs all night by lantern light, deep, under the platform, and sets the three jars in the earth one by one, and fills them in, and stamps the earth down, and you lie down on it again. You can feel them under you, cool, like three held breaths.

choices.text: Ask him what a glad day looks like

effects.log: "I have never seen one," he says, "so I do not know. But I will know it if it comes, and so will you." Then he digs. It is the most honest answer you have heard in a year.

choices.text: Refuse. A haechi keeps nothing for anyone

effects.log: The brewer bows and takes his jars home. Years later you hear that he buried them under his own house, and that the house burned, and the jars came through it, cracked, and the wine inside had turned to vinegar.

events.text: Three ministers stand at the edge of your platform, arguing about the jars under it. When is a good year? One says: a year of great harvest. One says: a year with no war on any border. The third, the youngest, says: a year when no lie is spoken in the council hall. Each says he means the good of the people.

choices.text: (the horn: true, true, and the third a lie) Look at the youngest

effects.log: He does not mean the people's good. He means his own: a year with no lies in the hall is a year he means to be the one deciding which words are lies. He goes red under your look. The other two, who are less clever, are honest.

choices.text: "A year when all three are true at once"

effects.log: They stop arguing and look at you, then at each other. "That has never happened," says the oldest. "No," you say. "That is why the wine is so good." They go away thinking about it, which is all you wanted.

choices.text: Say nothing. The jars will judge

effects.log: You put your chin on your forefeet, over the jars, and close your eyes. The ministers go on arguing for an hour and then go away, and the argument becomes a saying in the capital: as long as the jars under the haechi.

events.text: A night of rain. Someone is digging at the side of your platform, very quietly, with a trowel. When you turn your head it is a young man with the brewer's arms and none of the brewer's patience: the grandson. "The brewery is in debt," he says. "One jar. Only one. Grandfather would understand."

choices.text: (the horn: a lie, the last part) Put your forefoot over the hole

effects.log: Grandfather would not understand. Grandfather made him swear, on his deathbed, and he knows it. He sits down in the mud and cries, and you let him, and in the morning you send him to the king's steward, who needs a brewer for the spring rites, at a good price.

choices.text: Let him take one jar. Debts are real

effects.log: He takes one jar. The brewery is saved. Two jars remain under your feet for the glad day, and the grandson brings you bitter leaves every spring for the rest of his life, from guilt, which is a kind of thanks.

choices.text: Stand up and shake the rain off on him

effects.log: He flees, soaked. In the morning the hole is filled and smoothed by a guard who saw everything and says nothing. The jars are untouched. The grandson goes to work for another brewer and does well, eventually.

events.text: A great harvest, a year without war, and, by some accident of illness and retirement, a council hall where very few lies are being told. A young woman of the brewer's house comes to the gate with a spade and a question. "Is it a good year?" she asks you. "Good enough? You would know."

choices.text: "Not yet. Almost. Wait"

effects.log: She bows and takes the spade home. It is not a glad day: it is a lucky one, and a haechi can tell the difference. You settle down over the jars again. Somewhere ahead there is a year good enough, and you mean to be lying here when it comes.

choices.text: "Ask me in another hundred years"

effects.log: She laughs. "The family said you would say that," she says. She leaves the spade leaning on your platform, for whoever comes next.

choices.text: "Yes. Open one jar, and leave two"

effects.log: One jar comes up out of the earth, sealed and cold, and is opened on the broad road before the gate, and every passer-by is given a cup. It is the best wine anyone has ever tasted. Two jars stay under you, for a gladder day still.

events.text: A spark off the Fire Mountain on a dry northwest wind, and a thatched roof in the east market catches. By the time you are up off your stone, the house next to it is smoking too. The wind is rising. You have perhaps the time it takes to boil rice before this is a great fire.

choices.text: Run in and pull the burning thatch down with your teeth

effects.log: You drag the whole flaming roof off into the street and stamp it out, and then the next. Two houses lost, no more. Your mane smells of burned straw for a month. (-12 health)

choices.text: Roar the quarter awake and drive everyone to the canal with buckets

ok.log: Every door in the quarter opens at once. A chain of buckets from the canal, a hundred hands, and you at the head of it. Three roofs burn. The rest of the city sleeps through it.

fail.log: They wake, but too slowly, and the wind is quicker than buckets. By dawn the east of the city is ash, and the people stand in the smoke before the gate and look at you. (A great fire, -8 health)

choices.text: Let it burn the grain dealer's house. You know what he hides in it

effects.log: It burns, as fire does, his house and the two beside it, which were honest. You stand and watch, and the horn turns cold in your skull, at you. A haechi does not let fire judge. (-10 Clarity)

events.text: The bell at your throat goes off by itself in the dead of night: smoke. A spark has come over the river on a south wind and found the drying racks of the dyers' lane. The bell knows before you do. It is still ringing as you run.

choices.text: Keep ringing all the way down the road, and let the city wake

effects.log: A whole capital in the street in its sleeping clothes. The dyers lose a season of cloth and nothing else. In the morning the lane is blue and red with spilled dye and soot, like a painting of a fire.

choices.text: Silence the bell and fight it alone, quickly, before panic spreads

ok.log: You tear down the racks and drown them in the dye vats. Nobody wakes. In the morning the dyers find their lane soaked and stinking and saved, and a beast asleep in the middle of it. (-10 health)

fail.log: Alone was a mistake. By the time you let the bell ring, three quarters of the south are burning. (A great fire, -14 health)

events.text: A spark comes over the river, then another, then a rain of them, as if the Fire Mountain had sneezed. The roofs of the south quarter catch one after another like lamps being lit for a festival. There is only one thing that can swallow this much fire before morning, and it is lying on a stone before the palace gate.

choices.text: Go into the south quarter and swallow it, roof by roof

effects.log: By dawn your throat is a chimney and the south quarter is wet, black, and standing. The children come out into the street and stare at you, smoke coming gently out of your nose, and one of them claps. (-20 health)

choices.text: Stand on the bridge and swallow only what crosses toward the palace

effects.log: The palace is untouched. The south quarter is ash. You chose the walls you were set before over the roofs beyond them, and in the morning the whole city knows it. (A great fire, -10 health)

events.text: A fire in a moneylender's house in the middle of the night. The moneylender is out in the street in his sleeping robe, shouting to the neighbours that nobody is inside, nobody, so they should save his storehouse first: the silver, the pledges, the papers.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Go into the house, not the storehouse

effects.log: An indentured girl, locked in the back room so she will not run. You carry her out by her jacket and drop her in the neighbour's well bucket, quite gently. The storehouse burns, papers and all. Half the street's debts burn with it. Nobody mourns. (-12 health)

choices.text: Save the storehouse as he asks, then the house

ok.log: You drag the storehouse doors off and pull out his chests, and then go into the house anyway, because the horn is uneasy, and find the girl in the back room, coughing. Both saved. Only just. (-10 health)

fail.log: While you are hauling his chests, the fire jumps from the house to the next street. The girl gets out by herself through a window. The quarter does not. (A great fire, -12 health)

choices.text: Ring, roar, and let the street decide what to save

effects.log: The street saves the girl, whom they knew about, and lets the storehouse burn, which they also knew about. It is a better judgement than the moneylender's and very nearly as good as yours.

events.text: A spark on the roof of the county prison by the West Gate, and the old dry roof goes up like a torch. Inside, behind locked doors, are forty prisoners: thieves, debtors, two murderers, and, the horn has told you over the years as you passed, at least six who are there on lies. The jailer has the keys and is running away with them.

choices.text: Catch the jailer and take the keys

ok.log: You bring him back by the collar and he unlocks every door with shaking hands. Forty out into the street. Nobody runs, for once: they all stay to pass buckets. The prison burns alone.

fail.log: He gets away. You break the doors one by one with your shoulder. Forty out, all of them, and your shoulder never quite right again. The prison burns alone. (-15 health)

choices.text: Break the doors of the six you know are innocent first

effects.log: Six doors, then the rest. You know which six by the horn's memory, and the magistrate, who hears of it, sends for the six cases the next morning and finds the lies in every one. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let it burn. They are prisoners

effects.log: The six innocent and the two murderers die in the same smoke. Fire is no judge, and you knew it, and stood there. The horn will remind you of this for the rest of your life. (-10 Clarity)

events.text: The night of the lantern festival, with a hundred thousand paper lanterns in the streets and a wind getting up from the northwest. A spark from the mountain, or a candle, nobody will ever know, and the lantern rows over the main street go up one after another like a fuse.

choices.text: Run down the street knocking the lantern lines down into the gutters

effects.log: A beast tearing down festival lanterns at a dead run, the crowd parting and screaming and then cheering. The lines fall into the gutters and burn out on wet stone. The roofs never catch. (-10 health)

choices.text: Stand in the crossroads and get the crowd moving, before the crush kills more than the fire

ok.log: You lie down in the middle of the crossroads, very large, very calm, and the crowd flows round you like a river round a rock, out of the burning street, in good order. Nobody is trampled. The lanterns burn out overhead.

fail.log: The crowd moves, but slowly, and the lanterns light the eaves, and the eaves light the roofs. A quarter of the city burns on the festival night. (A great fire)

choices.text: Ring the bell once, so loud that the whole street stops and listens

effects.log: One note, and a hundred thousand people go silent. Into the silence you say, "Water." It is the only word you need. The festival ends early and wet, and is remembered for a hundred years as the year the haechi spoke.

events.text: A fire at the house of a man whose secret you have kept: a minister whose son is not his son, a truth you laid your horn down years ago so a family would survive. The hidden thing was dry wood after all. The house is burning, and the minister is in the doorway, looking at you, and he knows you know.

choices.text: Go in and put it out. A kept secret is still a promise

effects.log: You put out the house you once let stay dry. The son, who is not his son, helps you carry the water. In the morning the minister comes to the gate and says, very quietly, "Thank you for both." (-14 health)

choices.text: Put it out, and then tell the son the truth, gently

effects.log: The fire first; the truth after, in the wet ash, at dawn. The son listens to the end. Then he goes and sits with the minister a long time, and comes out still calling him father. Some dry wood is better burned off slowly. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let the wind take it. It was always going to burn

ok.log: The wind turns, by chance, and the house burns alone. Nobody else pays. You were lucky. You did not deserve to be. (-6 Clarity)

fail.log: The wind does not turn. A great fire starts in a house where you once laid a truth down, and goes everywhere. (A great fire, -6 Clarity)

events.text: Smoke from the potters' kilns outside the West Gate, and then not smoke but flame: a kiln left to fire overnight by a master who swears to the crowd that he banked it at dusk and went home to bed.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Look at the master, and then at the kiln door

effects.log: He did not bank it. He went to a drinking house. The crowd turns from the fire to him, and you turn them back to the fire, because a liar can wait and a kiln cannot. Two sheds burn. In the morning the master pays for them.

choices.text: Put out the kiln yard before it reaches the city wall

ok.log: Sand, earth, and your own broad back rolled over burning straw. The kiln yard is a ruin. The city wall, and the thatch behind it, is untouched. (-8 health)

fail.log: The straw stacks go up before you get there, and the sparks fly over the wall into the thatch of the West quarter. (A great fire, -12 health)

choices.text: Swallow the kiln, door and all

effects.log: A kiln's fire is a hard, tight, glazed fire, and it goes down like a hot stone. In the morning the potters find their kiln cold and every pot inside it perfect. They say it is the best firing in a few years. (-12 health)

events.text: A spark lands in the palace itself, on the roof of a hall at the back of the queen's quarters, and the old cedar shingles catch. You are at the corner in four bounds. There is a bronze water jar there, at the corner of the hall, full to the brim.

choices.text: Tip the jar over the eaves with your shoulder

ok.log: The jar goes over with a gong-like boom and a sheet of water hits the eaves. Steam, hissing, and then nothing. The cooks will tell this story for a hundred years: the jar did it, and the beast helped.

fail.log: The jar is heavier than a house. By the time it moves, the guards are there with buckets, and the fire is out, and you are standing very wet in a puddle. (-10 health)

choices.text: Hold the little flame-faced thing on the roof over the jar, so it sees its face

effects.log: There it is, crouched on the burning shingles, grinning: the fire demon's spark. You reach up, take it by the scruff, and hold it over the water. It looks, and shrieks, and goes out like a snuffed candle. The roof stops burning by itself.

events.text: Your horn is smoky, the city is dry, and the fire that comes tonight comes in three places at once: the east market, the paper lane, and the stables. The bell at your throat hums so hard it hurts. You cannot be in three places.

choices.text: The stables: horses cannot open doors

effects.log: Two hundred horses out into the night. The paper lane and the east market burn together, and by morning they are one burned place. (A great fire, -12 health)

choices.text: The east market: it is upwind of the rest

ok.log: Upwind, yes: put the east market out and the wind carries nothing to the others, and the city's own people manage the paper lane and the stables. You read the wind right. Three small fires, no great one.

fail.log: You read the wind wrong. It turns at midnight, and the paper lane takes the stables with it, and the stables take the north. (A great fire)

choices.text: Ring the bell for all three, and trust the city

effects.log: The city has learned to listen to you. At the first note, three quarters of the capital pour out with buckets, in three directions at once. You lie on your stone and ring until dawn, and nothing burns that matters.

events.text: A great fire is coming, and you know where: a sugar merchant's warehouse in the south quarter, packed with barrels of malt syrup and a lie about how much tax was paid on them. The spark has found it. Syrup burns like pitch. And the merchant is at the gate, on his knees, offering you anything, anything, to save his warehouse first.

choices.text: Ignore the offer. Save the lanes around the warehouse, and let it burn

effects.log: You make a ring of torn-down sheds and wet earth around the burning warehouse and let it burn inside it, a pillar of sweet black smoke all night. Nothing else catches. The merchant loses everything, which is not a sentence: it is only what was in the fire's way.

choices.text: Swallow the burning syrup, and then speak to the tax office

effects.log: It is the sweetest fire you have ever swallowed, and the worst for your horn. The warehouse is saved. So is the tax office's record, when you lie down on its step and tell it how many barrels there really are. (-18 health)

choices.text: Take his offer. Save the warehouse

effects.log: You save it, barrels and lies and all. He sends you a lacquer box of honey cakes every New Year after that, and every New Year your horn is a little cloudier. (A bribe: -8 Clarity)

events.text: The fire comes while you are asleep, a stone among stones before the gate, moss on your scales. The bell at your throat wakes you, ringing on its own. You lift your head and the moss cracks off you, and across the city a whole street is already a river of flame.

choices.text: Shake off the sleep and run

ok.log: Stiff from years of stone, you run anyway, and the city sees the stone beast before the gate get up and go into the fire. That is half the battle: they follow. The street is lost; the quarter is saved. (-10 health)

fail.log: Your legs are stone still. By the time they are flesh, the quarter is gone. (A great fire, -12 health)

choices.text: Do not run. Ring, and keep ringing, until the city wakes

effects.log: You lie where you are and ring, a stone beast with a bell, and the city comes out to the sound as if it had always known it would. The street burns. The quarter does not.

events.text: The drum sounds on the gate tower after midnight, and the one who beat it is {npc}, a young censor in a new black hat with your likeness embroidered on the front. {He} has sworn, {he} says, on taking the hat, not to tell one lie for a year. It is the third month. "It is impossible," {he} says. "Everyone at court lies. How do I answer them?"

choices.text: "Say less. Silence is not a lie"

effects.log: {npc} tries it. It works, mostly. By the end of the year {he} is known at court as the censor who says almost nothing, and when {he} does say something, the whole hall stops to hear it.

choices.text: "Answer them with the truth, and see who stops talking to you"

effects.log: Half the court stops talking to {npc}. The other half, it turns out, were waiting for someone to go first. {He} comes back at the end of the year with a list of friends half as long and twice as good.

choices.text: "Take off the hat until you are ready"

effects.log: {npc} looks at the hat in {his} hands a long time, then puts it back on. "No," {he} says. "Then I will never be ready." You lay your ears back, and {he} sees it, and walks home a little taller.

events.text: Someone beats the drum very softly, as if hoping not to be heard: {npc}, from the washers' quarter by the stream, with burned hands wrapped in rags. "My little brother set the fire in the tanners' lane," {npc} whispers. "By accident. A lamp. Nobody knows. If you tell, they will hang the boy. Do I have to tell?"

choices.text: "No. But the boy must carry water for the tanners until the lane is rebuilt"

effects.log: A year of carrying water for the people whose roofs the boy burned. The tanners never ask why. One of them, at the end of the year, gives the boy an apprenticeship. Some truths are better paid than told.

choices.text: Lower the horn. Tell {npc} to keep the secret

effects.log: {npc} weeps with relief and goes home. The lamp, the lane, the little brother: one more thing under one more floor in the capital, dry, and quiet. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: "Yes. Bring the boy here, and I will stand beside the two of you while it is said"

effects.log: The boy comes, shaking, and says it. You stand so close that the magistrate can see the haechi has already looked at this child and found no malice. It is a fine, and a year of labour, and nobody hangs.

events.text: The drum is not beaten tonight. Instead, at midnight, {npc} sits down on the step below your stone: a thief by the look of {him}, lean, quiet, with very good shoes. "I have been paid to steal your horn," {npc} says. "By a sect that grinds things. I am telling you because I have watched you for a month, and I do not think I can."

choices.text: "Thank you. Who paid you?"

effects.log: {npc} tells you: the name of a sect in the hills, the name of an elder, the price, which is insultingly low. In the morning the gate guard is doubled, and a sect in the hills finds that the capital knows its name.

choices.text: "Try, if you like. I will not move"

effects.log: {npc} laughs, softly. "That," {he} says, "is exactly why I cannot." {He} goes away down the broad road, and sends the money back to the sect, the story goes, wrapped in a chinaberry leaf.

choices.text: "Why are you a thief?"

effects.log: It is a long answer, and every word of it true. By dawn {npc} is not a thief, or at least has decided not to be one this year. {He} comes back sometimes to sit on your step and tell you how it is going.

events.text: {npc}, a leader of one of the court factions, a smiling courteous person in sky-blue silk, beats the drum by daylight with great ceremony and then speaks to you as one sensible creature to another. "Our enemies lie," {npc} says. "You know it. We know it. Let us bring them to you, one at a time, and you need only lower your head. We will take care of everything else."

choices.text: (the horn: true about the enemies, and a lie about everything else) Decline

effects.log: The enemies do lie. So does the faction, about what it means to do with them. "I will see your enemies," you say, "and I will see you, on the same day, in the same hall." {npc} stops smiling.

choices.text: "Bring them. And bring yourselves too"

effects.log: {npc} understands the offer exactly, and does not take it. A faction that wanted a leash has found a beast that bites the hand on it. You are spared their gifts for years, which is restful.

choices.text: Accept a gift as a token of goodwill

effects.log: A lacquer box of candied ginseng. Very sweet. Very cloudy, the next morning. The faction now holds a thread on you, and you can feel it in your horn like a hair caught in a comb. (A bribe: -8 Clarity)

events.text: {npc}, old now, beats the drum with a cane. Many years ago, {npc} says, {he} beat this same drum with bare hands, as a slave, at midnight, against a master who had stolen {his} family's land, and a beast with a horn got up and made the guard listen. "I am free now," {he} says. "I have land. I came to say: it was true, all of it, and I never thanked you."

choices.text: "You did. You came back"

effects.log: {npc} sits with you until dawn and tells you about the land: a hillside of barley, two oxen, a grandchild who reads. When {he} goes, {he} leaves a bag of barley on your step, which you do not eat, and do not let anyone take.

choices.text: "Tell me what happened after"

effects.log: Everything: the land, the lawsuit, the first harvest, the master's son who came to apologise thirty years later. A whole life that started with one beaten drum. You listen to the end. It is a better story than most of the ones the court tells.

events.text: {npc}, a warrior with burned forearms and a fire-axe on {his} back, beats the drum at dawn after a night of fire. "I fought beside you in the burning lanes," {npc} says. "I saw you go into the worst of it. I want to ask you one thing: are you afraid of fire? I am. Every time. I want to know if it ever stops."

choices.text: "No. It never stops. That is why we go"

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, as if a weight {he} has been carrying had been put down, not taken away. {He} comes back after every great fire for years, and sits on your step, and the two of you say nothing about being afraid.

choices.text: "I am not afraid of fire. I am afraid of what it is looking for"

effects.log: You tell {npc} about the kindling: the lies under the floors, the dry wood of a city. {He} is quiet a long time. "Then the axe is the wrong tool," {he} says. "No," you say. "It is one of them."

events.text: {npc}, a grandmaster of a fire art, comes to the gate with a sword of red steel and a reputation that walks in front of {him}. {He} does not beat the drum; {he} kicks it. "They say the Fire-Eating Haechi swallows any flame," {npc} says. "Mine is not any flame. Will you duel, or are you only a story?"

choices.text: Accept, and swallow the art

ok.log: The red sword comes down in a sheet of flame, and you open your mouth, and it goes in, and keeps going in, until {npc} is standing in the road with a cold sword and a very surprised face. {He} bows. It is a good bow.

fail.log: The art is real. You swallow most of it and the rest goes through your mane. {npc} sheathes the sword. "A story with teeth," {he} says, and goes away satisfied. (-18 health)

choices.text: "Swear before me that you came only to duel"

effects.log: {npc} swears. The horn goes cold: {he} came to see whether you could be killed, for a sect that would very much like to know. {He} sees the horn move, and goes pale, and leaves the capital that night, without a duel, with the answer.

choices.text: Lay your ears back. A haechi does not strike first at one who has done no wrong

effects.log: {npc} waits, sword drawn, for a fight that does not come. After an hour {he} sits down on the step. After two {he} starts talking. By evening {he} has told you about the master who taught {him} the art, and you have told {him} the master was lying about one thing, and {he} has wept.

events.text: {npc} comes to the drum at the dead of a winter night: a martial artist as old and strong as any human you have met, robed in plain grey. {He} does not beat it. {He} only says: "I have lived two hundred years, and everyone who could tell me the truth about myself is dead or afraid. You are neither. Tell me what I am."

choices.text: Tell {him}, exactly

effects.log: Some of it is splendid and some of it is very bad. You leave nothing out and add nothing. {npc} listens to the end without moving, and then bows to you, deeper than {he} has bowed to anyone in a century. "Thank you," {he} says. "Nobody has dared."

choices.text: "You already know. You came to hear someone say it"

effects.log: {npc} laughs, a short surprised bark. "Yes," {he} says. "Then say it." You do. It is shorter than {he} expected, and much worse, and {he} goes away lighter than {he} came.

events.text: Before the gate, in a cold dawn, you shake your head to clear it, and the horn does not ring. It knocks, like knuckles on a cracked jar. The crack you put in it, by lowering your head at an innocent, has been growing all winter, slowly, the way frost grows in a stone.

choices.text: Lie still and feel exactly where it runs

effects.log: From the root, a hair's width, a hand's length, toward the tip. Not through. Not yet. Everything the horn shows you now, you will see a little more faintly. Never falsely; only less.

choices.text: Go and find the one you wronged, whatever it costs

effects.log: You start that day. It will take a season, or a decade, or the rest of your life. A haechi that has butted an innocent does not get to decide how long forgiveness takes. (-6 health)

choices.text: Chew the bitterest leaf you can find, and hope

effects.log: The bitterness clears the horn, but it does not close the crack. Nothing closes a crack but the one it was made on. You know that. You chew anyway.

events.text: {npc} comes to the gate: the one you lowered your head at, years ago, and should not have. Older now, a little bent. {He} stands at the dismount line and looks at you for a long time. "I heard your horn cracked," {npc} says. "I wanted to see."

choices.text: Lower your head, not as a butt, but to the ground, and ask

ok.log: {npc} looks at the horn on the flagstones in front of {him}, and then, slowly, puts a hand on it. "It was a bad year," {he} says. "It is over." The crack closes under {his} palm with a sound like ice settling on a pond.

fail.log: {npc} looks at you, and then turns and walks back down the broad road. Forgiveness is not owed. You lie with your horn on the stones all day, and the crack stays, and {npc} was right to go.

choices.text: Say the truth plainly: "I guessed, and I was wrong, and you paid"

effects.log: {npc} nods. "Yes," {he} says. "I did." That is all. {He} does not forgive you, not today. But {he} comes back next spring, and stands at the line again, and looks.

events.text: The crack has settled in. When you shake your head the horn rings hollow, the warning every old haechi knows, and there are mornings when you look at a minister on the steps and cannot tell whether he is lying or only tired. Enough cracks would break it. Every case before the gate now feels like walking on spring ice.

choices.text: Point at no one this year. Let the horn rest

effects.log: A year without a single butt. The courts are slower. The city is a little drier. The horn is no better, but it is no worse, and it is the first year in a long time you have not been afraid of yourself.

choices.text: Point only when the horn is cold as winter, and never on a guess

effects.log: Three times this year the horn goes cold beyond any doubt, and three times you lower your head, and three times you are right. The rest of the time you lie still and let humans judge. They are not much worse at it than you are, these days.

choices.text: Sit the Stone Sleep and let the world go on without you for a while

effects.log: Stone to the brow. A crack does not close in sleep, but the fear in it does, a little. When you wake, the horn rings hollow still, and you are steadier when it does.

events.text: The magistrates of the capital have started to bring witnesses to the gate. Not the accused; the witnesses. Anyone who must swear to what they saw swears it in front of you, with the bell at your throat an arm's length away. It saves a great deal of time. The Board of Punishments asks whether it should be the law.

choices.text: Let it be the law: every oath in the capital sworn before the gate

effects.log: The Oath of the Bell. Witnesses stand before you in a line every morning, and the bell rings at perhaps one in twenty. False witness in the capital falls by half in a year. A hundred years later people still say "swear it before the bell" about anything that matters.

choices.text: Refuse. The courts must learn to see without you

effects.log: The Board is disappointed. But the magistrates who were leaning on you go back to their own eyes, and the good ones get better, and the bad ones are found out more slowly but more surely, by each other.

choices.text: Only for the poor, who cannot pay for a good advocate

effects.log: The rich hate it. The poor line up before dawn. Every case where a farmer's word stands against a landlord's, the farmer may ask for the bell, and the landlord must stand beside the farmer and swear too.

events.text: The state examination, held in the palace yard: ten thousand candidates under awnings, brushes, ink, and silence. The examiners have heard that candidates smuggle in crib-notes sewn into their sleeves and hats. The chief examiner asks if you would walk the rows.

choices.text: Walk the rows once, slowly, and let the bell decide

effects.log: You walk ten thousand desks. The bell shivers at two hundred and six. Two hundred and six sleeves are opened, and two hundred and five contain notes; the last contains a love letter, which the candidate is allowed to keep. The examination is cleaner than it has been in a century.

choices.text: Lie at the gate of the yard, where every candidate must pass you going in

effects.log: You do not need to walk the rows. Half the notes are thrown into the gutter outside before their owners reach you. The examiners collect a basketful of paper from the street, and the candidates who walk in past you walk in clean.

choices.text: Decline. A haechi does not mark examinations

effects.log: The chief examiner sighs. The examination goes on as it always has, with its cheats and its honest scholars mixed together, and you lie at the gate and watch the mountain, which has never yet sat an examination.

events.text: The market weights of the capital are a disgrace. Every merchant has two sets: one for buying, one for selling. The Board of Taxation proposes a standard set of bronze weights, kept at the gate, against which any weight in the city may be tried. The merchants' guild sends its elders to you, to say it is unnecessary, since all their weights are honest.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Lower your head at the guild elders, all of them

effects.log: Seven elders, seven lies. The bronze weights are cast that summer and kept on a shelf beside your stone, and any customer in the city may bring a merchant's weights to be tried. Within a year the second sets have been quietly melted down.

choices.text: Ask each elder to put their own weight on the scale beside the bronze

ok.log: Every weight is light. Every elder goes red. The guild votes for the bronze weights itself, the next week, to avoid the story getting about. The story gets about anyway.

fail.log: They bring the honest set, of course: they are not fools. The bronze weights are cast anyway, a year later, and the guild sulks.

choices.text: Change the market yourself: lie in the main market every day for a year

effects.log: A beast in the middle of the market, with a bell at its throat, every day for a year. Nobody asks you to judge anything. Nobody has to. The second sets of weights simply stop being used, in the way that whispering stops when a lamp is lit.

events.text: A woman of the capital comes to the gate with an accusation that would hang her neighbour: theft of a silver hairpin and a betrothal ring. Under the old law, a false accuser takes the punishment sought for the accused. The magistrate reminds her of it. She looks at your bell and goes very pale.

choices.text: (the horn: true about the theft, a lie about the ring) Say so, aloud

effects.log: The hairpin was stolen. The ring she gave back herself, and regrets. The neighbour pays for the hairpin and is not hanged, and the woman goes home without being punished for half a lie, which the magistrate decides, wisely, to call grief.

choices.text: Ask her to say it again, slowly, with the bell an arm's length away

effects.log: She starts again, and the second time she leaves out the ring. Nobody says anything. The neighbour pays for the hairpin. A city where people correct themselves in front of a bell is a cooler city.

choices.text: Let the old law work: she knows the cost

effects.log: She withdraws the whole accusation, hairpin and all, rather than risk it. The neighbour keeps both. Justice by fear is still a kind of justice, you suppose, but it is not the kind you are for.

events.text: Watch towers have gone up on every hill of the capital since the great fire, and on every one a watchman with a bell. They ring for cooking smoke, for mist, for nothing. The fire office asks you to teach them to read the Fire Mountain as you do.

choices.text: Teach them: the third peak, the leaning smoke, the northwest wind

effects.log: A winter of watchmen sitting in a row before your stone, learning the mountain. By spring the towers ring for real smoke and stay silent for mist, and the city learns to jump at their bells. You have made a hundred small haechi, without horns.

choices.text: Lend your bell to theirs: let every tower bell ring a little when yours does

effects.log: A sliver of you goes into each bronze bell on each hill. When yours hums at smoke, theirs hum too, faintly, all over the capital, and the watchmen wake before they know why. (-1 Clarity)

events.text: A new king, very young, asks you to come into the hall of audience on the first day of his reign and lie at the foot of the throne, where the ministers can see you. "Not to judge," the king says. "Only to be there. I want them to remember that something is listening."

choices.text: Go, for the first day only

effects.log: One day at the foot of the throne. The ministers speak more briefly than anyone can remember. On the second day you go back to the gate, and they speak at their usual length, but a little more carefully, for a year or two.

choices.text: Go, and stay for the whole first year

effects.log: A year at the foot of the throne. The young king learns, from watching which of his ministers will not look at you, more than any tutor could teach him. You go back to the gate in the spring with your horn tired and your mountain unwatched, and the young king a good deal older.

choices.text: "No. My place is facing the fire, not the throne"

effects.log: The young king is hurt, and then thoughtful. He has a painting of you hung behind the throne instead, ears laid back, horn high. The ministers spend his whole reign speaking with their backs to it, uncomfortably.

events.text: Two porters before your stone, shouting, each holding one end of a bolt of silk. Each swears the merchant gave it to him to carry, and the other stole it at the bridge. A small crowd has gathered. The gatekeeper looks at you and raises an eyebrow.

choices.text: (the horn: the taller one lies) Lower your head at the taller one

effects.log: The taller one lets go of the silk all at once, and his end hits the dust. The crowd cheers. The shorter one carries the silk away and comes back an hour later, alone, to bow.

choices.text: (the horn, faint through the crack: the taller one lies) Look only at him

effects.log: The mark is faint and true. You look at him, only look, and he breaks, as liars do when they feel themselves seen. The silk goes with the honest one.

choices.text: Lie still. Let them take it to the market judge

effects.log: Better no butt than a wrong one. They go off to the market judge still shouting. You never learn which one it was.

choices.text: Judge like a human: ask which of them knows the merchant's name

ok.log: Only one of them knows it. That settles it, without the horn, and you find you are rather pleased with yourself.

fail.log: They both know it: the merchant is famous. You guess, and lower your head, and it is the wrong one. Something in your horn cracks. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

events.text: A mother before your stone with her son by the ear. A jar of honey has gone from the kitchen, and the son swears the neighbour's boy took it. The neighbour's boy, standing a little way off, has honey in his eyebrows. So does the son.

choices.text: (the horn: both are lying) Lower your head at both, very gently

effects.log: Two small boys sat down in the dust by a horned beast, simultaneously. The mother laughs until she has to hold the gatekeeper's arm. Both are set to carrying water for a month, together, which is how they become friends for life.

choices.text: "The eyebrows have it." Say so, and nothing more

effects.log: The crowd looks at the eyebrows. Both boys confess at once, each blaming the other for the idea. Justice is done, very stickily.

choices.text: Lower the horn. Some cases are too sweet to judge

effects.log: You close your eyes. The mother sighs and takes both boys home by the ear, one in each hand. The horn does not even mind.

events.text: A minister's feast at the gate pavilion for an envoy, and you are invited, as a guest of honour, to lie at the foot of the table. Sweet rice, honey cakes, candied ginger, pine-nut gruel, all set before you on lacquer. The envoy, a smiling official of a neighbouring court, raises his cup and makes a speech about lasting peace.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie, the peace) Eat nothing, and look at the envoy

effects.log: The horn is cold all through the speech. The king, watching you not eat, watches the envoy too. A month later the border garrisons are quietly doubled, and the war the envoy's court was planning never quite happens.

choices.text: Eat the sweet things. It would be rude not to

effects.log: Delicious. The horn is clouded for a season, and you do not notice, during that season, anything about the envoy at all. Which, you realise afterwards, was the point of the honey cakes. (-5 Clarity)

choices.text: Ask for a chinaberry leaf instead, loudly

effects.log: A servant is sent running. The whole feast waits while a beast chews a bitter leaf at the foot of the table, and the envoy's smile gets a little fixed, and the speech about peace is shorter than it was going to be.
